pages.description: What Data Hub does, what it doesn't do, where your data shows up, and which page to read next.
pages.markdown:
# Overview (/docs/overview)



**For:** Everyone

Instrument data tends to stay where it was made. Files sit on the PC wired to the plate reader, named by whoever was at the bench, backed up if someone remembers. Finding a result from three months ago means knowing which machine made it and who was running it.

Data Hub moves that data off the instrument PC automatically. A small program called a watcher runs on each instrument PC, monitors its output folder, uploads new files as they appear, and groups them into runs. From then on the data is searchable in a browser, tied to the person who ran it, and reachable from a script or an AI agent without anyone copying files to a shared drive.

## What Data Hub isn’t [#what-data-hub-isnt]

Worth setting expectations early, because the name invites a few wrong guesses:

* It doesn’t change your raw files. Uploads are byte-for-byte, and processing only ever adds new files alongside them
* It isn’t an electronic lab notebook. Each run has a comment thread for notes and can link to the notebook pages where the experiment is written up, and that’s the extent of it
* It isn’t analysis software. It parses vendor formats into something viewable and downloadable; the analysis is still yours
* It doesn’t run on the instrument. Processing happens server-side after upload, so nothing competes with acquisition software for resources

## How a file becomes a run [#how-a-file-becomes-a-run]

1. A [watcher](/docs/concepts#watcher) on the instrument PC notices a new file in the folder it’s watching, waits for the file to stop changing, and groups it with the other files from the same acquisition into a [run](/docs/concepts#run).
2. The watcher uploads those files to cloud storage. For [supported instrument types](/docs/instrument-preprocessing), server-side code then reads the vendor’s format, pulls out settings like wavelength or imaging mode, and builds viewable versions such as plate maps or contrast-adjusted images.
3. The run appears in the web app, the REST API, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint at the same time. They’re three views of one record.

The full picture, including where each piece runs, is in [Architecture](/docs/architecture).

## Where your data shows up [#where-your-data-shows-up]

Four places in the web app, in the order most people use them:

* **Home**: every instrument’s recent runs together, with counts for today and this week, and today’s comments
* **Instruments**: one instrument’s runs, with columns matching what that instrument records, and a status badge that says whether its new files can arrive. Each instrument also has a watcher page for whoever maintains it
* **My runs**: runs you’ve claimed, so you can find your own work without filtering
* **Comments**: every run comment by day, filtered to your runs or to one instrument if you like

To see what has changed in Data Hub recently, open **Changelog** from the account menu.

If a term on those pages is unfamiliar, [Concepts](/docs/concepts) defines the vocabulary in one page. Run, watcher, run status, and instrument type are the four worth reading first.

## Get at the same data from code [#get-at-the-same-data-from-code]

The web app has no private back door. Everything it shows comes from a REST API that you can call yourself, and an MCP endpoint that AI clients can call on your behalf. Both read the same records, so a script sees exactly what the dashboard sees.

* **REST**: served at `/api/v1/` on your own deployment host. Each deployment publishes its own OpenAPI 3.1 document at `/api/v1/openapi.json`, so you can generate a client rather than hand-write one. See the [API overview](/docs/api)
* **MCP**: served at `/mcp/v1` over Streamable HTTP, and added to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or Cursor by pasting the URL. Agents can then search runs, read metadata, and fetch files during a conversation. Clients that support MCP Apps also show the same interactive run reports as the web app. See the [MCP overview](/docs/mcp)

The two differ in how you authenticate. REST clients carry a [personal access token](/docs/concepts#personal-access-token) that an admin creates in the web app, scoped and revocable. A token acts under its own name, so anything a script does is labeled with the token rather than with a person. MCP clients send you through a browser sign-in and a consent screen instead, then act as you with your own permissions, so nobody has to paste a credential into an AI client.

Typical uses look like pulling every run from an instrument for a batch reanalysis, writing the latest run’s archive to disk from a script, or asking an agent which plates from last week failed processing.

## What’s supported today [#whats-supported-today]

Nine instrument types have a processor, covering plate readers, gel docs, qPCR, TapeStation, FPLC, flatbed plate scanners, ND2 microscopy, DishCam time-lapse photos, and the Unchained Labs Aunty for protein melting temperature and particle size. [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing) lists what each one extracts.

An instrument without a matching processor still works. Its files upload, and you can search, claim, comment on, and download them. What you don’t get is extracted metadata, badges, or rendered previews. Adding a new type is a development task, not a settings change.

## Self-hosted by design [#self-hosted-by-design]

Data Hub isn’t a service you sign up for. Your team runs it, which is the point: raw instrument data and everything derived from it stay on infrastructure you control, and the source is open under the MIT license.

Running it means four pieces, deployed once by an engineer:

* The web app, which also serves the API and the MCP endpoint, on Vercel
* A PostgreSQL database for instruments, runs, files, and comments
* AWS S3 for the files themselves, split into raw and processed buckets
* An AWS Lambda that does the per-instrument processing and builds download archives

A Google OAuth client, created during that deploy, is the fifth piece and the one worth knowing about even if you’ll never touch the stack. It decides who can sign in at all: only your Google Workspace organization, or any Google account. Nothing inside Data Hub overrides that choice, so it’s a deployment decision rather than a setting an admin can change later.

Until the stack exists, nobody can sign in and no watcher can upload. The deployment runbooks live in the repository rather than on this site; [Deploy Data Hub](/docs/self-hosting) points to them.

## Getting access [#getting-access]

Sign in with your Google account, assuming it’s one the deployment allows. Everyone who signs in can browse instruments, runs, and files, comment on runs, and [send feedback](/docs/send-feedback) about Data Hub. Admins can additionally confirm instruments, issue tokens, promote other users, and connect Linear and Slack, and only an existing admin can grant you that. See [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles) for what each role can do.

## Start here [#start-here]

<Cards>
  <Card title="Deploy Data Hub" href="/docs/self-hosting" description="Engineers: the database, web app, and AWS stack." />

  <Card title="Set up an instrument" href="/docs/set-up-an-instrument" description="Operators and admins: go from a new PC to an uploading instrument." />

  <Card title="Browse and analyze runs" href="/docs/browse-runs" description="Everyone: find runs, claim your work, download files, and leave lab notes." />

  <Card title="Administration overview" href="/docs/administration" description="Admins: instruments, watchers, tokens, and members." />
</Cards>

## Reading these docs with AI [#reading-these-docs-with-ai]

Every page has a **Copy Markdown** button and a **View Options** menu. Use them to:

* Copy a page as Markdown into an assistant
* Open raw Markdown (`/docs/<path>.md`) or the dumps at [`/docs/llms.txt`](/docs/llms.txt) and [`/docs/llms-full.txt`](/docs/llms-full.txt)

pages.markdown:
# Deploy Data Hub (/docs/self-hosting)



**For:** Engineers

Data Hub is self-hosted, so nobody can sign in or install a watcher until your team has stood up the backend. This page is orientation only: what gets deployed, what access you need, and in what order. It doesn’t walk through the commands.

<Callout type="warn">
  For the actual deploy instructions, open [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md) in the data-hub repository. That guide has every command, env var, and checklist. Read this page first if you want the map before you start.
</Callout>

## What you’ll deploy [#what-youll-deploy]

Three pieces, each on infrastructure you choose:

| Piece                  | What it does                                                                              | Where it runs                            |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| PostgreSQL database    | Stores instruments, runs, files, watchers, and tokens                                     | Any PostgreSQL host, managed or self-run |
| Web app                | Serves the dashboard, the REST API, and the MCP endpoint                                  | Vercel                                   |
| Storage and processing | S3 buckets for raw, processed, and archived files, plus the Lambda that processes uploads | AWS, deployed with AWS SAM               |

You’ll also create a Google OAuth client, which is what actually controls who can reach your deployment. Data Hub has no invite flow and no email allowlist of its own, so that client’s setting is the whole access policy. Decide it deliberately and read [Who can sign in](/docs/security#who-can-sign-in) first.

Give `staging` and `production` separate databases and separate AWS stacks. They’re independent deployments holding independent data.

## Access you need before you start [#access-you-need-before-you-start]

The deploy stalls without all four, so confirm them up front:

* **Admin-level AWS credentials.** The first deploy creates the stack, which the automated deploy role can’t do. It can only update a stack that already exists
* **Vercel project access**, including permission to set environment variables for the environment
* **Google Cloud Console access** to create the OAuth client
* **GitHub repository settings access**, to store the secrets that let continuous integration handle every deploy after this one

You’ll also need the AWS CLI and the AWS SAM CLI installed locally.

## How the deploy is sequenced [#how-the-deploy-is-sequenced]

The web app and the AWS stack each need something the other produces, so the order matters. This is the sequence only; [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md) has the commands for each step:

<Steps>
  <Step>
    **Create the database** and keep its connection string. Make sure the host accepts connections from Vercel and from your continuous integration runners.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Deploy the web app**, set its environment variables, apply the database migrations, then sign in and create the access token the Lambda will use.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Bootstrap AWS resources**, once per AWS account rather than once per environment. This creates the shared resources both environments draw on.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Deploy the AWS stack** for this environment, using the web app’s URL and that token.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Wire the AWS outputs back into the web app**, then redeploy so it picks them up.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Expect the web app to deploy cleanly at step 2 and still not work. Anything touching files, uploads, reprocessing, and run archives stays broken until step 5 connects it to AWS. A green deployment is not the finish line.

## Things that catch people out [#things-that-catch-people-out]

These failures account for most lost time on a first deploy:

* **Set `ADMIN_EMAILS` before you sign in for the first time.** It’s what promotes the first admin. Sign in before setting it and you get an account with no permission to create tokens or confirm instruments
* **Point `BETTER_AUTH_URL` at this deployment’s own public origin.** Data Hub builds the Google callback URL from it, so a value copied from another environment sends people to that other host and sign-in fails. AI clients read the same value when they sign in over MCP, so a wrong one breaks them too
* **Google sign-in on Vercel preview deployments needs `OAUTH_PROXY_URL` and `OAUTH_PROXY_SECRET`.** Google matches each redirect URI exactly and every preview gets a new URL, so previews route the callback through one stable deployment whose URI is registered. Production registers its own and leaves both variables unset
* **Create the Lambda’s token from the Lambda preset.** The Lambda checks an instrument’s type before choosing a processor, so without `instruments:read` every upload fails on a permission error rather than an obvious misconfiguration. DishCam processing also reads the run’s file list, so it fails without `runs:read`. The **Lambda** preset includes both
* **Set `ENABLE_S3_FILES` to `true` or `false` for the AWS stack.** An empty value fails the deploy. Use `false` unless you want the Lambda to read very large files from a mounted copy of the raw bucket, which needs a VPC and costs extra; the runbook covers turning it on later
* **Bootstrapping fails if the AWS account already has a GitHub identity provider** from an unrelated project. Reuse the existing one instead of creating a second
* **Set `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` before an admin saves Slack or Linear secrets.** Data Hub encrypts those secrets with it, and saving fails without it. Generate one with `openssl rand -hex 32`
* **The Slack channel webhook and the Linear connection aren’t environment variables.** A workspace admin sets them under **Settings → Integrations** after the deploy; see [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations). The Slack app credentials for direct messages can be either environment variables or saved there. Feedback stays turned off until an admin connects Linear

## What finished looks like [#what-finished-looks-like]

Operators can install watchers and instruments start uploading. Hand them [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument), and create their first tokens through [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). To turn on feedback reports and Slack messages, an admin then follows [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations).

From then on, deploys are automatic. Merges deploy the web app, apply migrations, and ship the Lambda, so this manual sequence runs once per environment.

## The runbooks [#the-runbooks]

The deploy commands live next to the code in the data-hub repository. Start with [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md):

* [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md): the full sequence above, with every command
* [Continuous integration and deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/ci-and-deployment.md): how later deploys, migrations, and watcher releases happen
* [Local development](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/local-development.md): run the app on a laptop, including a setup that needs no AWS or Google credentials
* [Architecture for contributors](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/architecture.md): internals

For a product-level map of the components and how data moves between them, rather than deploy steps, see [Architecture](/docs/architecture).

pages.title: Set up an instrument
pages.description: Go from a fresh instrument PC to an active instrument uploading runs into Data Hub.
pages.markdown: # Set up an instrument (/docs/set-up-an-instrument) **For:** Lab operators and admins This walkthrough takes you from nothing to an uploading instrument: create an access token, install the watcher, register the instrument, get an admin to confirm it, then start watching. CLI flags, the full config schema, and Windows service setup each have their own page; this guide links them once. Data Hub is self-hosted. The web app, PostgreSQL database, and AWS stack (S3 plus the processing Lambda) must already be running. If they are not, an engineer needs the [Deploy Data Hub](/docs/self-hosting) guide first. ## Before you start [#before-you-start] You need: * **The watch directory**: the folder your instrument writes output into. * **File patterns**: globs to upload, for example `*.csv`, `*.xlsx`, `*.tiff`. * **[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)** installed on the instrument PC (it manages Python for you). To make setup and maintenance easier, we recommend setting up remote access to the instrument PC via [Windows Remote Desktop](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/remote/remote-desktop-services/remotepc/remote-desktop-allow-access). ## 1. Create an access token [#1-create-an-access-token] The watcher authenticates to Data Hub with a personal access token. Only workspace admins can create tokens, so ask an admin if you are not one. In the Data Hub web app, go to **Settings → Access Tokens** and click **Create token**. Give the token a **Name** that identifies the instrument PC, for example `Plate Reader PC`. Set **Expiration** to “No expiry”. (The token can always be revoked if necessary.) Under **Scopes**, click the **Watcher** preset. It grants only what a watcher needs: registering, reporting runs, and uploading files. Click **Create token**, then copy the token. It starts with `dhub_` and is shown only once. Keep the token handy: you paste it into the setup wizard in step 3. For rotation, revocation, and the full scope list, see [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). ## 2. Install the watcher [#2-install-the-watcher] On the instrument PC, install the watcher with `uv`. The `windows-service` extra adds `pywin32` so you can follow [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service), which is the default on a lab PC: ```sh uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]" ``` On macOS or Linux, omit the extra: ```sh uv tool install data-hub-watcher ``` Full install, verify, and update steps live in [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher). ## 3. Run the setup wizard [#3-run-the-setup-wizard] Start the wizard with `data-hub-watcher init`. It prompts you for one thing at a time: Choose the environment. For a live lab, this is production. Enter your Data Hub API URL e.g. `https://datahub.your-domain.com/api/v1`. Paste the token from step 1 when it asks for the API key. The wizard checks the key, then lists the instruments already registered. Pick your instrument from the list, or choose **Register a new instrument** if it is not there. For a new instrument, enter an ID and a display name. The ID is a short, lowercase, hyphenated name like `bio-rad-cfx96`. **It cannot be changed later.** Enter the full path to the folder your instrument writes into. List which files to upload, such as `*.pcrd,*.csv`. The watcher ignores files that do not match. Choose how files get grouped into runs. Pick the preset that matches how your instrument names its output, or write your own. The wizard previews a few matches so you can check the run IDs. For example, the default preset uses the filename prefix before the first underscore, so `RUN001_quant.csv` and `RUN001_melt.csv` both group into run `RUN001`. Set the stability period. This is how much time (in seconds) a file must stay unchanged before the watcher counts it as finished. The default is 5 seconds; raise it for instruments that write large files slowly. Choose the upload mode. “Auto” uploads each file as soon as it is stable; “Manual” waits for your approval first. For run detection options, see [Configure run detection and uploads](/docs/configure-run-detection); [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection) lists every preset. The wizard then registers the watcher, saves the config to `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` (`C:\Users\\.data-hub\config.yaml` on Windows), and syncs it to Data Hub. When it reports that setup is complete, start watching. ## 4. Confirm the instrument’s registration [#confirm-the-instruments-registration] A pending instrument cannot upload to Data Hub until an admin confirms it from the web app. Until then its badge reads **Pending**, and its page shows a **Waiting for confirmation** card in place of the runs table. Members see one line saying the instrument is waiting for an admin. Open the Data Hub web app and navigate to **Instruments > View all** from the app sidebar. Select the “Pending” tab and find your instrument. It should show an amber **Pending** badge. Click **Confirm…**. A window shows what the watcher registered: the computer, the watch folder, the file patterns, how files become runs, and the upload mode. Check that it matches what you entered in the wizard. If it doesn’t, choose **Change settings first** to fix it. Choose an **Instrument type**, which is required, then click **Confirm instrument**. The instrument moves to the “Active” tab. The instrument’s badge reads **Connecting** until the watcher service is running and checks in, which step 5 starts, and then **Online**. Start the service within 15 minutes of confirming: after that, the badge turns **Offline** with the notice “The watcher never checked in” until the watcher’s first check-in. Open the instrument’s page and check the watched folder and file patterns shown under its name. They should match what you entered in the wizard; files outside that folder, or with names that don’t match a pattern, won’t reach Data Hub. Admins can change an instrument’s type later: open the three-dot menu, select **Edit details**, and pick a supported type. What each type produces is in [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing). Adding a new processor requires code changes; see [Adding a new instrument](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/lambda.md#adding-a-new-instrument) in the developer docs. See [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments) for more info. ## 5. Start the watcher service [#start-the-watcher-service] First, preview what the watcher will do without starting it: ```sh data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run ``` This validates config, checks that the API is reachable and the instrument is active, and previews which files would be picked up. When it looks right, install and start the watcher as a Windows service. Run these from an **Administrator** terminal: ```sh data-hub-watcher service install data-hub-watcher service start ``` The service starts on boot, keeps running after you log out, and auto-updates in the background. Lifecycle and log details are in [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service). On macOS or Linux, run the watcher in the foreground instead: ```sh data-hub-watcher watch ``` The watcher detects new files, groups them into runs, uploads them (in auto mode), and sends a heartbeat every 60 seconds. Runs appear in the dashboard after upload. ## What you get once it is running [#what-you-get-once-it-is-running] * Raw files upload to cloud storage * Instrument runs and files appear in the web dashboard * Watcher service automatically restarts on PC restart * The watcher’s activity, health, and settings appear on the instrument’s **Watcher** page, and the instrument’s badge shows whether new files can arrive * Subscribed users can get in-app and Slack notifications for new runs

pages.title: Browse and analyze runs
pages.description: Use the web app to find runs, check that new files will arrive, inspect processed results, claim attribution, download files, comment, and manage run lifecycle.
pages.markdown: # Browse and analyze runs (/docs/browse-runs) **For:** Everyone After instruments are uploading, the web app is where you find runs and act on them: inspect results, claim work, download files, and leave lab notes. The sections below follow the order you’ll use them in. ## Orient yourself in the app [#find-a-run] The sidebar and the home page are the two starting points for daily work. **Home** lists recent runs across instruments, most recent first, with counts for today and this week at the top. The **Runs needing attention** card beside them counts runs whose upload failed, whose processing failed, or whose processing stalled, of any age. When it isn’t zero, choose it to list those runs. Filter by date range, who ran it, and instrument-specific metadata when it’s available, then page through results. Below the runs, Home shows up to four of today’s comments; use the date picker to see comments from a different range. **Instruments** in the sidebar lists five instruments, and **View all** opens the full list. Each instrument’s page starts with its name and a status badge that says whether new files can arrive; see [Check that new files will arrive](#check-files-will-arrive). Under the name are the folder its watcher reads from and the file patterns it uploads, then a runs table with column filters that match the instrument type (for example wavelengths on a plate reader). **My runs** lists runs you’ve claimed, so you can return to your own work without re-filtering the full dashboard. Its **Runs needing attention** card counts only your runs. **Comments** lists every run comment by day. Open it from **View all comments** on Home. Each person’s profile page also shows the comments they wrote and the comments on runs they ran. ### Narrow a long run list [#narrow-a-long-run-list] Home and the instrument pages share the same four controls: * **Search runs**: filters the list by run name as you type * **Date range**: presets from Today through Last 4 weeks, plus a custom range. Home shows today’s runs until you pick another range, and **All time** shows every run * **Add filter**: filter by run status, or turn on **Show deleted runs** * **Column headers**: sort by **Run Started**, **Last Updated**, size, who ran it, or any instrument-specific column The **Lab Notebook** column header filters the list to runs that have a [lab notebook link](#lab-notebook), or to runs that don’t. **Run Started** is when the instrument acquired the run. **Last Updated** changes when the run’s files change, or when someone edits, claims, or comments on it, or changes its lab notebook links. The default order is newest run first. The sort order is saved in the page link, so a link you share opens with the same order. ### What each run status means [#run-status] A run’s status tells you how far its files have got from the instrument to the dashboard: | Status | Meaning | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Failed | At least one file failed processing. The file’s row on the run page gives the reason. | | Stalled | At least one file has been processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing. Reprocess it to try again. | | Upload failed | The watcher gave up on at least one file, for example because its folder is no longer on the instrument PC. See [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). | | Waiting to upload | Files are on their way from the instrument PC: someone requested them, or the watcher uploads them on its own. | | Uploaded | The files are in storage. Processing hasn’t started, or this instrument type has no processor. | | Queued | You chose **Reprocess**, and the files are waiting for a free processing slot. They start as other files finish. | | Processing | The server is reading the files, extracting metadata, and building reports. | | Not uploaded | Some files are only on the instrument PC, and nothing will upload them until someone requests them. Common on instruments in manual upload mode. | | Completed | Processing finished. | | Empty | The run has no files. | A run with files in several states shows the first status in this table that applies. For example, a run with one failed file and nine completed files shows **Failed**, and a run with three processed files and 285 that nobody requested shows **Not uploaded**. **Waiting to upload** and **Not uploaded** replace the earlier **Pending upload**. A saved link or API call that filters by `pending` still works and matches both. ## Check that new files will arrive [#check-files-will-arrive] If a file you saved on the instrument PC hasn’t shown up, start with the badge beside the instrument’s name. It says whether new files can reach Data Hub. The same badge appears in the instruments table, on Home, and in search results. | Badge | What it means | | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Online** | New files upload automatically. For an instrument in manual upload mode, new files upload when someone requests them. | | **Restarting** | The instrument PC is restarting or updating. This usually takes a minute or two, and you don’t need to do anything. | | **Connecting** | The watcher was just set up and hasn’t checked in yet. If it hasn’t checked in after 15 minutes, the badge turns **Offline**. | | **Offline** | New files won’t appear right now. A notice under the instrument’s name says why. | | **Pending** | An admin hasn’t confirmed this instrument yet. Admins see a card in place of the runs table; members see one line. | | **Retired** | The instrument no longer takes new runs. Its runs stay browsable. | Hover over the badge, or focus it with the keyboard, for a short explanation. Select it to open the instrument’s watcher page, where anyone signed in can read its activity, health, and settings. Only admins can change anything there. The watcher is the program on the instrument PC that finds new files and uploads them; [Concepts](/docs/concepts#instrument-status) has the full rules for each badge. ### When the badge reads Offline [#when-offline] A red notice sits between the instrument’s name and its runs. It says what happened in plain words: | Notice | What happened | | ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **New files aren’t being picked up** | The watcher is running but can’t find its watch folder, which the notice names. An admin can choose **Change folder** to fix it. | | **The watcher isn’t checking in** | The watcher hasn’t checked in for 5 minutes, or didn’t come back within 15 minutes of a restart. The notice says when it last did. The PC may be off, or the watcher may have crashed. | | **The watcher never checked in** | The watcher was set up, but no check-in arrived within 15 minutes. Its service may not be running on the PC, or the PC can’t reach Data Hub. | | **Uploads from this instrument are paused** | Someone stopped the watcher on the PC. New files appear once it’s started again. | | **This instrument isn’t connected to a watcher** | The instrument never had a watcher, or its watcher was deregistered, which the notice dates and credits. Admins can choose **Connect a watcher**, which opens [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). | **See details** opens the watcher’s **Activity** tab. Members see only that link, and none when there is no watcher to look at. Tell an admin what the notice says, or send them the link: the [troubleshooting guide](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#instrument-shows-offline) covers each reason. An instrument in manual upload mode, whatever its badge says, shows a blue note beside its file patterns: “Files upload when someone requests them.” That isn’t a problem. Files wait until someone chooses **Upload**; see [Request an upload](#request-upload). ## Search the workspace [#search] Press **⌘ K** (macOS) or **Ctrl K** (Windows/Linux) to open global search from any page. Results are grouped into runs, files, instruments, users, and comments. That means you can also look up a colleague’s work or the text of a lab note. A file hit opens the parent run with the files table already filtered to that file. Runs also match on their [lab notebook links](#lab-notebook). Paste a notebook page’s URL to find every run linked to it, or search for a link’s label. ## Open a run and inspect results [#open-run-detail] Each run has a details page at `/instruments/your_instrument_id/runs/your_run_id`. The arrows beside the run name step you to the next or previous run without going back to the list. The top of the page lists who ran it, the number of raw files, and their total size. Below that, the **Lab notebooks** section links to the notebook pages for the experiment; see [Link a run to its lab notebook](#lab-notebook). What you see after that depends on the instrument type and whether a processor ran: * Metadata tags for extracted fields, such as experiment type, wavelength, or temperature * Processed reports such as tables, images, PDFs, and videos, including interactive plate maps for plate readers and a video player for DishCam runs * A files table of everything in the run, labeled Raw or Processed, with each file’s size and status Click a metadata tag to open the instrument’s runs table filtered to that value. For example, clicking a wavelength tag lists every run on that instrument recorded at the same wavelength. Reports with many images, PDFs, or spectra show one item at a time. Search by filename to jump anywhere in the run, or use the arrows to step through it. The counter beside the arrows shows your position out of the total. Plate maps with more than 12 columns, such as 384-well plates, scroll sideways inside the plate. Per-type inputs and outputs are in [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing). ### Filter the files table [#filter-files] The files table has separate **Type** and **Status** filters. Use them to show, for example, only failed files or only processed CSVs. **Download all** and the run archive include only the files the filters show. ### Live file updates [#live-file-updates] While files are uploading, queued, or processing, the run page checks for updates every 5 seconds for up to 5 minutes. After that it stops and shows **Stopped checking for file updates**. Choose **Refresh** to check for another 5 minutes. Uploading or reprocessing files from the page also starts a new 5 minutes. ## Claim who ran it [#claim-who-ran-it] Use **Claim** on the run details page to attribute yourself. You can claim or unclaim your own user only, so nobody else can attribute a run to you. Claims show on the run and appear in “ran by” filters on Home and elsewhere. API tokens can’t claim runs; a signed-in person has to. ### Asked after a download [#claim-prompt] When you download a run archive or a file from a run nobody has claimed, Data Hub asks **Did you run this?** in a card near the bottom of the page. Choose **I ran this** to claim the run, or **Not me** so that browser doesn’t ask about the run again. Downloading several runs from a runs list asks once about all the unclaimed ones, and **I ran these** claims them all. An AI assistant connected to the [MCP server](/docs/mcp) learns the same thing when it downloads from an unclaimed run, so it can ask you and claim the run for you. ## Link a run to its lab notebook [#lab-notebook] A run can link to the lab notebook pages for its experiment, so whoever analyzes it can read how it was set up. Any web page works, such as a Notion or Google Docs page. On the run page, choose **Add link** in the **Lab notebooks** section, paste the page’s URL, and give it a label if you like. Without a label, the link is named after the last part of its URL, which for a Notion page is its title. Tick **I ran this run** to claim the run at the same time. Each link shows who added it and when; use its **⋯** menu to edit, copy, or remove it. * A run can have up to 20 links, but only one to each page. * Two URLs count as the same page when they differ only in `http` or `https`, `www.`, a trailing slash, the part after `#`, or tracking parameters such as `utm_source`. Notion links count as the same page when they have the same page ID, so a link copied before the page was renamed still matches. * Anyone signed in can add, edit, or remove any link. * A deleted run keeps its links, but they can’t change until the run is restored. Runs tables show each run’s first link in the **Lab Notebook** column, with **+1**, **+2**, and so on when there are more. Filter that column to **No link** to find runs that still need one. To link many runs at once, select them and choose **Add notebook link**; see [Act on several runs at once](#bulk-actions). Scripts can manage links through the [REST API](/docs/api) with a token that has the `runs:link` scope. An AI assistant connected to the [MCP server](/docs/mcp) can add, edit, and remove them with the `add_notebook_link`, `update_notebook_link`, and `remove_notebook_link` tools. ## Download files [#download-files] From the files table you can: * Preview a CSV, TSV, JSON, or other text file by clicking its row. The preview shows the first 1 MB of the file. Use the back and forward buttons to move between previewable files on the same page of the table. **Download** in that window saves the file * Select files and choose **Download** in the bar that appears above the files table. One file downloads directly. Two or more come as a single zip, which builds in the background like **Download all** * Choose **Download all** to build a zip of active files in the run, with any active file filters applied Large zips build in the background. When one isn’t ready yet, Data Hub tells you how long to wait before trying again. ## Act on several runs at once [#bulk-actions] Select the checkbox on one or more run rows to open an action bar at the bottom of the list. Run rows have no buttons of their own; every run action goes through this bar. * **I ran these**: claim every selected run in one step * **Remove my attribution**: unclaim them * **Upload**: ask the watcher to upload files that are still on the instrument PC. Data Hub refuses the request for a run whose instrument isn’t **Online** or **Restarting**, and a message says how many failed; see [Request an upload](#request-upload) * **Download**: download a zip of each selected run * **Reprocess**: run server-side processing again, including on runs whose files have stalled * **Add notebook link**: link every selected run to the same [lab notebook](#lab-notebook) page. Runs that already link to it keep their link and are skipped * **Remove notebook link**: choose from the links on the selected runs, and remove them from every selected run * **Delete**: mark the selected runs deleted **Upload**, **Download**, **Reprocess**, **Delete**, and the notebook link actions appear only when every selected run allows them. For example, **Reprocess** is hidden if one of the selected runs belongs to an instrument type with no processor, and the notebook link actions are hidden if a selected run is deleted. **Remove notebook link** also needs at least one selected run to have a link. The notebook link actions work on up to 100 runs at a time. The checkbox in the header row selects every run on the page, and **Clear** drops the selection. The selection stays when you move to another page of the same results. It clears when you change the search, a filter, or the sort, so the bar never acts on runs from a list you are no longer looking at. The files table on a run page works the same way: select files to get **Upload**, **Dismiss**, **Reprocess**, and **Download** for just those files. Its **Upload** follows the instrument’s badge, like the other [Upload buttons](#request-upload). Its selection also clears when you change the files search, a filter, or the sort. ## Comment on a run [#comment] The comments thread on run details is for lab notes and follow-ups. Comment activity can notify people who claimed the run or already commented, and clicking a comment notification scrolls to that comment. Set preferences under **Settings → Notifications**; see [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications). Only the author of a comment can edit it. Authors can delete their own comments, and workspace admins can delete any comment. Comments posted by a script through an API token show the token’s name with a key icon instead of a person. ## Reprocess or delete a run [#reprocess-and-delete] Reprocessing runs server-side processing again. Use it after a file failed or stalled, or after an engineer fixes the code that reads a file type. The stored result doesn’t change until you reprocess. * On the run page, hover over a file and choose **Reprocess**. * To reprocess several files, select them in the files table and choose **Reprocess** in the bar. * To reprocess whole runs, select them in a run list and choose **Reprocess** in the bar. Reprocessing sends only the original instrument files. Files Data Hub generated, such as videos, previews, and CSVs, have no **Reprocess** button and are rebuilt from the originals. Reprocessed files go through a queue; see [How reprocessing is queued](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-queue). **Delete** marks the run deleted without removing stored files. To find a deleted run again, turn on **Show deleted runs** under **Add filter**, then open it and choose **Restore**. Anyone signed in can delete or restore a run. Files that were queued for reprocessing when the run was deleted stay queued and don’t start while the run is deleted. If you restore the run, they start as processing slots free up. Deleting a run also cancels the uploads that were requested for its files, so the watcher stops trying to send them. Those files go back to **Not uploaded**. Restoring the run doesn’t bring the requests back. Choose **Upload** again if you still want the files. See [Request an upload](/docs/browse-runs#request-upload). While a run is deleted, Data Hub refuses a watcher’s reports of it, so the watcher’s new files aren’t added. After you restore the run, restart the watcher to send them, or choose **Upload** on a file to have the watcher send that file without a restart. Watchers before 1.4.3 also send them when another file of the run finishes. See [A run was deleted on Data Hub](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#a-run-was-deleted-on-data-hub). ### How reprocessing is queued [#reprocess-queue] Reprocessing starts at most 10 files at a time, counted across all runs and instruments. When you choose **Reprocess**, each file goes into a queue: * A file that can start right away shows **Processing**. * A file that has to wait shows **Queued**. It starts when another file finishes, and files that were queued earlier start first. * A run with queued files shows **Queued** in the runs list, unless a file in it failed, stalled, couldn’t upload, is waiting to upload, or is uploaded and not yet processing. * If Data Hub can’t send a file to the processor, or the processor ends with an error without saving a result, the file shows **Failed** with a message that says so, and the next queued file starts. Reprocess the failed file to try again. * To take the waiting files out of the queue, choose **Cancel queued** at the top of the run page. Each queued file shows **Failed** with a message that says the reprocess was cancelled, and you can reprocess it again. Files that have already started aren’t affected. Files that arrive from a watcher upload count toward the 10, but they start right away and never wait in the queue. A file that has been processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing stops counting, so one stuck file doesn’t hold up the queue. A large run takes several rounds. For example, reprocessing a run of 80 files starts 10 files, and the other 70 show **Queued** until slots open. You can leave the page, because the queue keeps running. A queued file has no **Reprocess** button. An admin who runs Data Hub can change the limit with the `PROCESSING_CONCURRENCY_LIMIT` variable; see the [web application environment variables](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/getting-started.md#web-application). If a file that the queue started never finishes, for example because Data Hub restarted just as it started the file, it shows **Stalled** after 20 minutes. The queue then puts it back in line once. If it stalls a second time, it stays **Stalled** until you reprocess it. ### Request an upload [#request-upload] A file that the watcher found but nobody requested reads **Not uploaded**. Choose **Upload** on that file to ask the watcher to send it, or **Upload all** at the top of the **Files** section to ask for every file in the run that is **Not uploaded** or **Upload failed**. A requested file reads **Uploading** until it arrives, and the watcher picks up the request within a minute. On instruments that upload automatically, this needs watcher 1.2.1 or later; see [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds). The footer under the files table counts how many files are waiting on the instrument PC, how many couldn’t upload, and how many are uploaded. On an instrument that uploads automatically, a new file reads **Waiting to upload** until the watcher sends it. This needs watcher 1.4.5 or later; with an older watcher the file reads **Not uploaded** for the minute or two before it arrives. The **Upload** and **Upload all** buttons on a run page follow the instrument’s badge. When one is turned off, the reason shows beside it: | Badge | Upload buttons | Beside them | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Online** | On | Nothing | | **Restarting** | On. Requests wait until the watcher is back | “The instrument PC is restarting. Uploads start once it’s back.” | | **Connecting** | Off | “The watcher hasn’t checked in yet.” | | **Offline** | Off | “Can’t upload while the watcher is offline.” | | **Pending** | Off | “This instrument is waiting for an admin to confirm it.” | | **Retired** | Off | “This instrument is retired.” | If the badge reads **Offline** and the run has files that are still on the instrument PC, a red notice sits above the **Files** section. It says how many files are still on the PC, which watcher isn’t running, and when it last checked in, and links to **See details**. A run with no waiting files never shows the notice, whatever the badge says. Data Hub keeps a request made while the instrument is **Restarting** and the watcher uploads the files once it’s back. If no heartbeat arrives for about 15 minutes, Data Hub cancels the request and the files read **Not uploaded** again. The **Upload** button on a runs list doesn’t follow the badge. Select runs and choose it to ask for every waiting file in them. For an instrument that is **Offline**, **Connecting**, **Pending**, or **Retired**, Data Hub refuses that run’s request, and a message reports how many runs failed. Choose **Upload** from the run page instead to see why. For instruments in [manual upload mode](/docs/concepts#upload-mode), every file waits for this approval. **Dismiss** tells the watcher not to upload a file. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads). ### When an upload fails [#upload-failed] The watcher gives up on a file when it can’t send it. The file then reads **Upload failed**, and hovering over the status shows why: * **The folder is no longer on the instrument PC.** Someone renamed or moved the run’s folder after the watcher found it. The files under the new name usually arrive as a new run, so look for a run with the same start time and a similar name. * **The file isn’t on the instrument PC.** The folder is there but the file was moved or deleted. * **The upload kept failing.** The watcher tried and the upload failed each time, usually a network problem. The message shows the last error. * **The path is outside the watch folder.** The watcher won’t upload a file outside the folder it watches. For a requested file, the watcher checks three times, about a minute apart, before it gives up. On an instrument that uploads automatically, it gives up as soon as an upload fails, and it tries again the next time it starts. A red notice above the **Files** section lists the files that couldn’t upload, one block per reason and folder. Each block says why and when the watcher gave up. Once the cause is fixed on the PC, choose **Upload again** in the block, or **Upload** on a single file, to try again. If the files are gone for good, choose **Dismiss these files**. The run reads **Upload failed** until every such file is uploaded or dismissed, and the watcher’s activity shows one “Couldn’t upload” entry per run and reason. Whoever requested the files gets one notification per run and reason, in the app and, if they connected Slack, as a direct message. See [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications). Marking files **Upload failed** needs watcher 1.4.5 or later. An older watcher puts the file back to **Not uploaded** instead, without a reason; see [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds). ## Use the same data outside the UI [#programmatic-access] You can also list and fetch the same runs and files over the [REST API](/docs/api) or the [Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint](/docs/mcp). REST needs a [personal access token](/docs/concepts#personal-access-token); scopes and creation are covered in [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). MCP clients sign in through the browser instead, and clients that support MCP Apps show the same interactive run report you see here.

pages.title: Instrument data preprocessing
pages.description: What Data Hub does to a raw file after upload, which instrument types have a processor, and what supporting a new instrument takes.
pages.markdown: # Instrument data preprocessing (/docs/instrument-preprocessing) **For:** Lab operators, admins, and engineers After a [watcher](/docs/concepts#watcher) uploads a raw file, Data Hub can run a **preprocessor** on it: code that reads the vendor’s file, pulls out settings like wavelength or imaging mode, and builds something you can look at in the browser. Nine instrument types have one today. This page covers what each produces, why a file sometimes gets no processing, and what adding a new instrument involves. Support for a new instrument isn’t a settings change. It takes a new Python module, a database migration, an edit in two repositories, and a Lambda redeploy. See [Add support for a new instrument](#add-support-for-a-new-instrument). ## How a file reaches a processor [#how-preprocessing-works] 1. A file arrives in raw storage, which triggers the Lambda. The bucket notifies on every upload, with no per-instrument filtering. 2. The Lambda checks the filename against a **filename gate**, a cheap test that skips files no processor wants before making any API call. 3. It reads the instrument, then looks up a processor by the instrument’s [type](#set-the-instrument-type). Unmapped types stop here. 4. The processor reads the file, extracts metadata, writes processed files when it has any, and updates the run through the API. 5. The file’s status moves from `processing` to `completed` or `failed`. ### Why an upload sometimes produces nothing [#why-an-upload-produces-nothing] Two silent no-ops explain a file that uploaded and then produced nothing. Neither marks the file failed, because nothing went wrong: * **The filename missed the gate.** Each type accepts a narrow pattern, listed in the table below. A TapeStation run only triggers on its PDFs, so the peak-table CSVs it writes are stored but don’t start processing on their own. * **The instrument has no type set, or a type with no processor.** Files upload and stay browsable; you get no metadata and no reports. Filename gates apply to uploads only. Choosing **Reprocess** in the web app skips the gate, because clicking it states your intent. That’s why a file that produced nothing on upload can still process when you reprocess it by hand. ### Set the instrument type [#set-the-instrument-type] Processing is chosen by the instrument’s **type**, not by its instrument ID. The ID (`azure-cielo-qpcr`) names one physical machine. The type (`qpcr`) names a vendor’s file format, and several instruments can share one. To set it, open the instrument page as an admin, choose **Edit details** from the three-dot menu, and pick an **Instrument type**. One type means one vendor’s output format. Names like `qpcr` and `fplc` read as generic, but each is bound to a single vendor’s parser: `fplc` expects ÄKTA PDFs, `qpcr` expects Azure Cielo exports. Typing a different vendor’s instrument into an existing type feeds files to a parser that can’t read them. Supporting a second vendor means splitting the type, which is a code change. ## Supported instrument types [#supported-instruments-at-a-glance] | Type | Vendor and model | Gate for uploads | You get | | -------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `tape_station` | Agilent 4150 TapeStation | `.pdf` | Tape-type badge, PDF reports | | `fplc` | Cytiva ÄKTA FPLC | `.pdf` | PDF you can read on the run page, no metadata | | `gel_doc` | Azure 600 Gel Doc | `.tif`, `.tiff` | Contrast-enhanced PNG, imaging badges | | `qpcr` | Azure Cielo qPCR | `.csv`, `.pdf`, `.aze` | Dye-channel badges, melting curves, the instrument’s PDF report | | `epson_v700_scanner` | Epson V700 Scanner | `.tif`, `.tiff` | Plate preview JPG, colony measurements | | `hina_microscope` | Hina Microscope (Nikon ND2) | `.nd2` | Channel overlay JPG, a video of each timelapse, channel badges | | `plate_reader` | SpectraMax iD3 and iD5 | `.xls` | Well-data CSV, interactive plate maps | | `dishcam` | DishCam time-lapse camera | `.tif`, `.tiff`, `run.json` | A video of each photo stack, camera-setting badges | | `aunty` | Unchained Labs Aunty | `.xlsx` | A plate with a curve chart in each well, experiment badges | ## Agilent 4150 TapeStation [#agilent-4150-tapestation] Reads the tape type out of peak-table CSV filenames and shows TapeStation reports on the run page. * **Expected files**: CSVs named like `YYYY-MM-DD - HH-MM-SS-_peakTable.csv`, plus matching PDFs * **Metadata**: `Tape Type`, for example `gDNA` or `HSD1000`, when the filename matches that pattern * **Processed files**: none * **On the run page**: tape-type badge, a PDF viewer, and peak-table reports Uploads trigger on the PDF, not the CSV. A run of CSVs alone stays unprocessed until you reprocess it by hand. ## Cytiva ÄKTA FPLC [#akta-fplc] Stores ÄKTA chromatography PDFs so you can read them in the browser. The processor reads nothing out of the PDF itself yet, so this type gets no badges or filters. * **Expected files**: `.pdf` reports from the ÄKTA * **Metadata**: none * **Processed files**: none * **On the run page**: files table, plus each PDF embedded under Report Data A newly seeded FPLC stays `generic` on purpose until an operator has checked its output format. ## Azure 600 Gel Doc [#azure-600-gel-doc] Rebuilds each gel TIFF as a viewable image and reads the imaging settings the instrument recorded. The processor stretches intensities to the 1st to 99th percentile, per RGB channel or as grayscale, then lays every page of the TIFF side by side in one 300 dpi PNG. The stretch is cosmetic: it makes faint bands visible on screen and doesn’t change the raw file. * **Expected files**: TIFF from the Azure 600 * **Metadata**: `capture_type`, `imaging_mode` (true color, fluorescence, or chemiluminescence), `wavelengths`, `colors`, read from the TIFF `XPComment` tag * **Processed files**: contrast-enhanced PNG * **On the run page**: imaging badges, files table, image viewer for the PNGs Those metadata fields also drive the column filters on the instrument page. ## Azure Cielo qPCR [#azure-cielo-qpcr] Reads dye channel names, melting curves, and the instrument’s PDF report. * **Expected files**: * the Cq Values CSV, for dye channels * the melting curve CSV (a name ending in `_MeltingCurve.csv`) * the PDF report the instrument writes * `.AZE` project files * **Metadata**: `dye_channels`, the unique names in the Cq Values CSV’s `Fluorescence` column * **Processed files**: `{run_id}_melting_curve_derivatives.csv` and `{run_id}_melting_curve_plate.json` from the melting curve CSV. An `.AZE` file produces `{run_id}_aze_melting_curve_derivatives.csv`, `{run_id}_aze_melting_curve_plate.json`, and `{run_id}_aze_experiment.json`. * **On the run page**: dye-channel badges, the PDF report under **Report Data**, and a **Melting Curves** section The **Melting Curves** section shows the plate for one dye channel at a time. Click a well to see its melting curve and derivative, with a dashed line at the melting temperature. A run with more than one PDF gets previous and next buttons under **Report Data**. The other CSV files a qPCR run writes upload normally and show as completed, but contribute no metadata. ### `.AZE` project files [#aze-project-files] Data Hub reads melting curves from the Azure Cielo’s native `.AZE` project files as well as from the CSV export. Melting temperatures match the CSV export, but other values can differ. That’s because `.AZE` files store raw fluorescence, while the CSV export can be adjusted for baseline. A project with no melt data completes with no processed files. The watcher uploads `.AZE` files only when `*.AZE` is in the instrument’s file patterns. An admin can add it on the **Settings** tab of the instrument’s watcher page (watcher 1.4.0 and later); see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). With an older watcher, add it on the instrument PC with `data-hub-watcher config edit` and restart the watcher. Patterns are case-sensitive, so match the case the instrument uses. See [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference#field-reference). ## Epson V700 Scanner [#epson-v700-scanner] Finds agar plates in a flatbed scan and measures the colonies on them. The processor looks for plates sitting in gold 3D-printed frames. For each plate it finds, it crops the plate, then detects colonies: crop the edge, compare against the plate background, apply a difference-of-Gaussians filter, threshold, and measure whatever survives. Measurements come out in physical units, so colony areas are comparable between scans. * **Expected files**: TIFF plate scans * **Metadata**: `dpi`, `color_mode`, `plate_count`, `plate_boxes`, plus `colony_detection` summaries when colonies were measured * **Processed files**: a web-sized JPG with plate outlines and colony boxes drawn on, and a `_colonies.csv` of per-colony area, centroid, eccentricity, and mean RGB * **On the run page**: scanner badges, files table, and reports for the processed CSV When no plates are found, you still get a resized JPG of the whole scan, and colony detection is skipped. An empty `plate_count` usually means the frames weren’t recognized rather than that the plates were blank. ## Hina Microscope [#hina-microscope] Turns each Nikon ND2 into a composite image you can view in the browser, and each timelapse into a video. Every channel is reduced to one 2D frame per time point (a maximum projection over Z, the first index over position), stretched to the 1st to 99th percentile, then composited onto a brightfield background in each channel’s fluorophore color. The processor reads one frame at a time, so large stacks process without loading the whole file. * **Expected files**: ND2 * **Metadata**: `sizes`, `channels` (name, excitation and emission wavelength, color), and `dimensions`. Each timelapse file also records `frames`, `frame_interval_ms` (the measured time between frames), and `playback_fps` in its own file metadata. * **Processed files**: an RGB overlay JPG of the first time point for every file in the run, plus an MP4 for every file with more than one time point * **On the run page**: channel and size badges, files table, and a viewer with one item per file. A timelapse plays as a video, with its JPG shown before you press play. Any other file shows its JPG. A timelapse video plays at the capture rate or at 10 frames per second, whichever is faster, so slow captures stay watchable. A file that doesn’t record the time between frames plays at 10 frames per second. Each channel’s contrast comes from the first frame and stays the same for the whole video, so brightness doesn’t flicker and the first frame matches the JPG. Pixels that later grow brighter than the brightest 1% of the first frame show at full brightness, so a signal that grows strongly during the capture can look saturated. If the video can’t be made, for example because the timelapse can’t finish within the [15-minute processing limit](#when-processing-fails), the file shows **Failed** and the message says why. The JPG and the raw file are still available. A timelapse processed before Data Hub made videos gets its video when you choose **Reprocess** on the file or on the run. Timelapses take several minutes each, so reprocessing a run with many of them shows most files as **Queued** while 10 process at a time. Channel layout is identical across a Hina run, so metadata is written once by whichever file finishes processing first. Later files still get their JPG and skip the metadata write. Reprocessing one file therefore won’t correct run metadata if the layout changed mid-run. An image too large to preview at full size gets a smaller preview instead. For example, a 6221 × 6221 pixel image is previewed at 3110 × 3110 pixels. The raw file is unchanged, and you can download it at full size. A file that showed **Failed** for this reason earlier gets its preview when you choose **Reprocess** on the file or on the run. Two kinds of image still show **Failed** instead of a preview: an image from a color camera, which Data Hub can’t preview yet, and an image far larger than the Hina Microscope has produced so far. The message on the file says which. In both cases the raw file is stored and you can download it. ## SpectraMax iD3 and iD5 plate readers [#spectramax-id3-and-id5-plate-readers] Both models share one processor, which converts SoftMax Pro exports into the well data behind the interactive plate maps. * **Expected files**: SoftMax `.xls`, which is UTF-16 text with a `Plate:` header rather than a real Excel workbook * **Metadata**: `measurement_mode` (Absorbance, Fluorescence, or Luminescence), `measurement_type` (Endpoint, Kinetic, Spectrum, or Well Scan), and `wavelengths` as bare numbers with no unit suffix * **Processed files**: `{run_id}_raw_well_data.csv` * **On the run page**: wavelength, mode, and type badges, plus plate maps built from that CSV What the plate map shows depends on the read: * **Kinetic** reads get a time slider. Reads that skip the edge wells keep their time values, and runs that SoftMax Pro stopped early still process. * **Spectrum** reads (wavelength scans) get a wavelength slider. * **Luminescence** reads show no wavelength, because luminescence doesn’t use one. SoftMax Pro writes `#SAT` in a saturated well and `#Low` when the flash lamp missed a well. Those wells show as blank on the plate map, and the rest of the file processes normally. ## DishCam [#dishcam] Turns each DishCam photo stack into a video you can play on the run page. * **Expected files**: multi-page TIFF photo stacks, plus the `run.json` file the camera writes next to them * **Metadata**: camera settings from `run.json`: `fps`, `measured_fps`, `frames`, `duration_seconds`, `quality`, `format`, `started`, and `finished` * **Processed files**: an MP4 video and a JPEG still frame for each stack * **On the run page**: a video player at the top of the report, with play, pause, and a timeline you can drag. The still frame shows before you press play. The video plays at the capture rate or at 10 photos per second, whichever is faster, so slow captures stay watchable. The stored `fps` metadata still records the real capture rate. A stack processes once both the stack and its `run.json` are in storage, in either order. When a run gathers captures from several folders, each stack uses the `run.json` from its own folder. Watcher 1.1.0 and later keep every folder’s `run.json`, renaming later copies with a short tag such as `run~3f9a1c2b.json`. See [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds). Large stacks are read one photo at a time. If a stack can’t finish within the [15-minute processing limit](#when-processing-fails), it shows **Failed**, and the message says how far through the photos it got. You can still download the raw file. ## Unchained Labs Aunty [#unchained-labs-aunty] Reads Aunty exports, which measure protein melting temperature and particle size, and draws a plate of curves. * **Expected files**: the `.xlsx` export from the Aunty software. Thermal ramps, sizing runs, isothermal holds, and exports that contain only the results table without curves all process. * **Metadata**: `experiment_type` (`thermal_ramp`, `sizing`, or `isothermal`), `experiment_count`, and the first experiment’s settings: `analysis_mode`, `start_temp_c`, `end_temp_c`, `rate_c_per_min`, `temperature_c`, `analysis_version`, and `experiment_name` * **Processed files**: `{run_id}_aunty_curves.csv`, with every curve point for every well, and `{run_id}_aunty_plate.json`, which drives the plate view * **On the run page**: a plate with a small chart in each well. Click a well to open its full chart. On the instrument page, filter Aunty runs by experiment type, analysis mode, temperature, and ramp rate. ## Types with no processor [#instruments-without-a-matching-processor] `generic` and `instant_raman` have no processor, and neither does an instrument whose type is unset. Those uploads still work: files are stored, and you can browse, search, claim, comment on, and download them. What you don’t get is extracted metadata, badges, filters, or processed artifacts. Leaving a new instrument as `generic` is the safe default. It keeps data flowing while someone confirms which processor, if any, can read its files. ## When processing fails [#when-processing-fails] A file with status `failed` carries an error message on the run page. Open the run, then choose **Reprocess** on that file, or select runs in a run list and choose **Reprocess**. See [Reprocess or delete a run](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-and-delete). Processing one file has a 15-minute limit. A file that hits the limit, or is too large to process at all, shows **Failed** with a message that explains why. The raw file stays in storage, and you can download it. A file that stays in processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing shows **Stalled**. That usually means the processor stopped without reporting back. Reprocess it to try again. Reprocessing puts a file in a queue and starts at most 10 files at a time. A file that has to wait shows **Queued** until a slot opens. See [How reprocessing is queued](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-queue). Reprocessing is also the fix after an engineer corrects a parser: the code changed, but the stored result didn’t, until you ask for it again. ## Add support for a new instrument [#add-support-for-a-new-instrument] **For:** Engineers Adding an instrument type is a development task spanning the web app and the Lambda, not a configuration change an admin can make in the dashboard. Budget for a database migration and a Lambda image deploy. **Add the type.** Extend `instrumentTypeEnum` in `web/lib/db/schema.ts` and generate an `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE` migration. Reuse an existing type only when the new instrument writes the same vendor’s format. **Write the processor.** Add a module under `lambda/src/data_hub_lambda/` exposing `process_file(instrument_id, run_id, filename)`, which reports progress through the Data Hub API. **Register it twice.** Add the type to `PROCESSORS` in `lambda/src/data_hub_lambda/processors.py`, with its filename gate, and to `PROCESSABLE_INSTRUMENT_TYPES` in `web/lib/instruments/processable-types.ts`. These two lists have to agree: the Lambda uses the first to dispatch, and the web app uses the second to decide whether to offer **Reprocess**. **Add tests** for the processor and for the registry gate. **Deploy the Lambda image.** No new S3 trigger is needed, since the raw bucket already notifies on every upload. You can exercise a processor locally without S3 or API access using the `data-hub-process` CLI, and drive the whole handler against a local S3 mirror with its `handler` subcommand. Full detail, including the archive builder and the Docker build, is in [the Lambda developer docs](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/lambda.md#adding-a-new-instrument--processor).

pages.title: Configure notifications
pages.description: Choose in-app and Slack notifications for new runs, instruments that go offline, comments, failed uploads, service messages, and feedback, including per-instrument subscriptions and personal Slack direct messages.
pages.markdown: # Configure notifications (/docs/configure-notifications) **For:** Everyone Data Hub can notify you in the app and in Slack when new runs arrive, when an instrument goes offline, when someone comments on a run you care about, when files you requested couldn’t upload, when a script sends you a message, and when feedback you sent is closed. Open **Settings → Notifications** while signed in. Everything on that page is a personal choice that affects only you. Connections that the whole workspace shares, such as the Slack channel for new runs and the Slack app behind direct messages, are under **Settings → Integrations** and only admins can change them. See [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations). In-app and Slack preferences are independent: you can turn on either channel for a type without turning on the other. ## In-app preferences [#in-app-preferences] | Setting | Effect | | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Mute new-run notifications** | Suppresses new-run notifications in the bell for every instrument. Offline alerts and your per-instrument choices stay as they are. | | **Instruments that go offline** | Notify when an instrument you subscribe to has been offline for 30 minutes, and again when it’s back online. See [When an instrument goes offline](#instrument-offline). | | **Comments on runs you ran** | Notify when someone comments on a run you are attributed to. | | **Replies to your comments** | Notify when someone comments on a run you previously commented on. | | **Uploads that failed** | Notify when the watcher gives up on files you requested, for example because their folder is no longer on the instrument PC. You get one notification per run and reason. See [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). | | **Service notifications** | Show messages that integrations and scripts send you through the API. | | **Updates on your feedback** | Notify when a [feedback report](/docs/send-feedback) you sent is resolved or declined. | | **New feedback** | Admins only. Notify when someone sends feedback about Data Hub. | ### Per-instrument subscriptions [#per-instrument-subscriptions] Under **Per-instrument**, toggle the instruments you want to hear about. A subscription covers the instrument’s new runs and its outages. **Mute new-run notifications** silences only the new runs, so your subscriptions still bring offline alerts while it’s on. You can also subscribe from the notifications switch on an instrument’s page, or from the instruments table’s notifications column when that column is shown. ### When an instrument goes offline [#instrument-offline] When an instrument you subscribe to shows **Offline** for 30 minutes in a row, Data Hub tells you once, with the reason from the [notice on its page](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher). When its badge is **Online** again, you get a second notification that says how long it was offline. * Every reason counts: the watch folder is missing, the watcher stopped checking in, never checked in after it was set up, or was stopped, or the instrument has no watcher. * A routine Windows restart or automatic update shows **Restarting** and doesn’t alert. A restart that doesn’t come back within 15 minutes turns **Offline**, and the 30 minutes start then. * You get no reminders while it stays offline. A change of reason during the outage doesn’t send a second alert. * Retiring the instrument ends the outage without a message. ## The notification bell [#notification-bell] The bell icon in the app lists recent notifications: * New runs are grouped by day and instrument, and each group expands to show its runs. * Clicking a comment notification opens the run and scrolls to that comment. * A failed-upload notification says how many files couldn’t upload and why, and opens the run. * An offline or back-online notification names the instrument and opens its page. * Messages sent by a script through an API token show the token’s name with a key icon. ## Slack direct messages [#slack-direct-messages] Connect your Slack account on the same settings page to receive matching events as personal direct messages. After connecting, choose which types also go to Slack: * New instrument runs, for the instruments you subscribe to. The new-run mute applies only to the bell. * Instruments that go offline, for the instruments you subscribe to * Comments on runs you ran * Replies to your comments * Uploads that failed * Service notifications * Updates on your feedback * New feedback (admins only) Disconnect or reconnect from the same card. You have to connect with your organization’s Slack workspace; Data Hub rejects any other workspace. If **Connect to Slack** is missing or doesn’t finish, an admin hasn’t set up the Slack app yet. See [Slack app for direct messages](/docs/integrations#slack-app). ## Workspace Slack channel [#workspace-slack-channel-admins] The shared Slack channel that gets a message whenever a new run is created is set by admins under **Settings → Integrations**. See [Slack channel for new runs](/docs/integrations#slack-channel). ## Set up the Slack app for personal DMs [#set-up-the-slack-app-for-personal-dms] The Slack app setup, including scopes, redirect URLs, and where to enter its credentials, is in [Slack app for direct messages](/docs/integrations#slack-app).

pages.title: Send feedback and see what’s new
pages.description: Report a bug or request a feature about Data Hub from the app or an AI assistant, follow the report’s status, and read the in-app changelog.
pages.markdown: # Send feedback and see what’s new (/docs/send-feedback) **For:** Everyone Use **Feedback** to tell the team that runs Data Hub about a bug, a missing feature, or anything else about the app itself. Each report becomes an issue in your workspace’s Linear, and Data Hub tells you when that issue is closed. Feedback is for problems with Data Hub. A problem with one run’s data, such as a wrong plate map, belongs in a comment on that run, where the people who ran it will see it. ## Send a report [#send-a-report] Open the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar and choose **Feedback**. Pick a **Type**: **Bug**, **Feature request**, or **Other**. Enter a **Title** and a **Description**. Say what you expected and what happened instead. Optionally open **More details** and fill in **Trying to do**, **Tool**, and **Error message**. Choose **Send feedback**. Data Hub also records the page you were on, so you don’t need to paste a link. If you send a report with the same title within 24 hours, Data Hub returns the report you already sent instead of creating a second one, unless that report has been closed. The **Feedback** item appears only after an admin connects Data Hub to Linear. If you don’t see it, ask an admin to follow [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations#linear). ## What happens to a report [#what-happens-to-a-report] * Data Hub creates an issue in the Linear team your admins chose, with the label they picked for that type of report, if any. * The team works on the issue in Linear. * When the issue closes, Data Hub sends you a notification, and a Slack message if you turned that on. A report’s status follows its Linear issue: | Linear issue | Report status | | ---------------------------------- | ------------- | | Completed, such as **Done** | Resolved | | Canceled, or closed as a duplicate | Declined | | Anything else | Open | The notification names the Linear status too, such as **Resolved (Done)** or **Declined (Duplicate)**. Turn it on or off with **Updates on your feedback** under **Settings → Notifications**; see [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications#in-app-preferences). You hear about a report once each time it closes. Moving the issue from one closed status to another doesn’t notify you again, but reopening and closing it does. ## Send feedback from an AI assistant [#from-an-ai-assistant] AI assistants connected to Data Hub over [MCP](/docs/mcp) can send feedback for you, for example when a tool call fails. The assistant shows you the draft first and sends it only after you agree. It can also list the reports you sent and read one in full, by report ID or by Linear issue ID such as `ENG-1476`. The tools are listed under [MCP tools](/docs/mcp/tools). API tokens can’t send feedback, because every report needs a person behind it. Scripts that call `POST /api/v1/feedback` have to use a signed-in session. ## Who sees which reports [#who-sees-which-reports] Members see only the reports they sent. They can list them through the API or an AI assistant, without the Linear assignee, priority, or activity. Admins review every report under **Settings → Feedback**: * **Open** and **Closed** are separate tabs. * Each row shows the Linear issue ID, status, label, priority, and assignee. * A report’s detail includes the Linear status changes and comments, and an **Open in Linear** link. Status changes happen in Linear. Data Hub has no control for changing a report’s status. Admins can also turn on **New feedback** under **Settings → Notifications** to hear when someone sends a report. ## See what’s new in Data Hub [#changelog] Choose **Changelog** in the account menu to see what has changed in Data Hub, newest first. It opens on top of the page you’re on. Each entry shows its title, and you select a title to read the entry. Entries you haven’t seen before are marked **New** and start open. If none are new, or every entry is new, only the newest entry starts open. A dot on your account button means there’s an entry you haven’t seen yet, and opening the Changelog clears it. Many entries link to the page on this site that covers the change. To share an entry, open it and select **Copy link**.
