Anyone signed in to your Data Hub who opens the link sees the Changelog with that entry open. Someone who isn’t signed in has to sign in first and then open the link again. An AI assistant connected to Data Hub [gives the same links](/docs/mcp#questions-about-data-hub) when it tells you what changed.

pages.title: Install and update the watcher
pages.description: Install, reinstall, verify, and manually update the Data Hub watcher on an instrument PC across operating systems.
pages.markdown:
# Install and update the watcher (/docs/install-the-watcher)



**For:** Lab operators

Install the watcher on an instrument PC, verify it, and apply manual updates. Fleet auto-update (what admins advertise and how PCs upgrade in the background) is covered in [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

## Prerequisites [#prerequisites]

* **[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)**: recommended. It installs Python for you; you do not need a separate Python install.
* **A personal access token** starting with `dhub_`. Admins create these at **Settings → Access Tokens**; members cannot mint their own. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).
* **Watch directory** and **file patterns** for the instrument output folder.

## Install [#install]

Most lab instrument PCs run Windows, so install the `windows-service` extra by default. It adds `pywin32`, which the watcher needs for the [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service) setup:

```sh
uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]"
```

This puts the `data-hub-watcher` CLI on PATH in an isolated venv managed by `uv`.

On macOS or Linux, or on a PC you will only run in the foreground, omit the extra:

```sh
uv tool install data-hub-watcher
```

## Configure [#configure]

```sh
data-hub-watcher init
```

The wizard walks through environment, API key, instrument, watch directory, file patterns, run detection, stability period, and upload mode. New instruments start as `pending` until an admin confirms them; see [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument).

Config saves to `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` and syncs to the server. Intent-level guidance for detection and uploads is in [Configure run detection and uploads](/docs/configure-run-detection); every field is in [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference).

## Verify [#verify]

```sh
data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run
```

Dry-run validates config, checks API reachability and instrument status, and previews matching files without starting the monitor.

## Run [#run]

On a lab PC, run the watcher as a Windows service so it starts on boot, survives logout, and auto-updates in the background. From an **Administrator** terminal:

```sh
data-hub-watcher service install
data-hub-watcher service start
```

Lifecycle commands, log locations, and recovery settings are in [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service).

For a one-off check, or on macOS or Linux, run in the foreground instead:

```sh
data-hub-watcher watch
```

The watcher monitors the directory, waits for files to stabilize, groups them into runs, uploads (or queues in manual mode), and heartbeats every 60 seconds. Stop a foreground watcher with `Ctrl+C`; stop the service with `data-hub-watcher service stop`.

## Reinstall [#reinstall]

Reinstall the same package (for example after a broken venv or missing service extra):

```sh
uv tool install --reinstall data-hub-watcher
# or with the Windows service extra:
uv tool install --reinstall "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]"
```

On Windows services, follow with `data-hub-watcher service reinstall` from an Administrator shell so the service and upgrade Scheduled Task point at the new install.

## Change configuration later [#change-configuration-later]

```sh
data-hub-watcher config edit   # re-prompt each field
data-hub-watcher config open   # open the YAML in your editor
data-hub-watcher config show   # print the current config
```

Changes sync to the server automatically.

## Manual update (`self-update`) [#manual-update-self-update]

Use this when you want an upgrade immediately, or on a non-service install. Background fleet upgrades are described in [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

```sh
data-hub-watcher self-update            # check + upgrade if needed
data-hub-watcher self-update --check    # report status only
data-hub-watcher self-update --force    # re-run even if versions match
```

The command asks the API for the latest published version and upgrades according to how the watcher was installed:

| Install method                | Upgrade flow                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Windows + `uv tool install`   | Routes through the `DataHubWatcherUpgrade` Scheduled Task. The CLI returns when the task accepts; the service restarts automatically. Tail `~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log` for progress. |
| POSIX + `uv tool install`     | `uv tool install --reinstall data-hub-watcher==<latest>` inline. **Restart the watcher** afterward.                                                                                       |
| Plain venv `pip install`      | `pip install -U data-hub-watcher==<latest>` inline. **Restart the watcher.**                                                                                                         |
| Editable / `uv sync` checkout | Refused; upgrade with `git pull && uv sync`.                                                                                                                                              |

<Callout type="warn">
  On Windows uv-tool installs, `data-hub-watcher service install` (or `service reinstall`) must have run once from an Administrator shell so the upgrade Scheduled Task exists.
</Callout>

### Pin a specific version [#pin-a-specific-version]

```sh
uv tool install data-hub-watcher==1.2.1
```

Some features need a minimum watcher version, such as uploading files larger than 5 GB (1.2.0) or **Request upload** on instruments that upload automatically (1.2.1). Check [What each version adds](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds) before pinning an older version.

Run `self-update --check` to confirm the server’s advertised target. When the server’s latest moves past your pin, the next auto-update tick tries to upgrade again. Fleet-wide pins and rollbacks are admin actions under [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

pages.title: Run as a Windows service
pages.description: Install and operate the Data Hub watcher as a Windows service so it starts on boot, survives logouts, and can auto-update in the background.
pages.markdown:
# Run as a Windows service (/docs/windows-service)



**For:** Lab operators

On a lab instrument PC, run the watcher as a Windows service. This is the default setup: the service starts on boot, keeps running after you log out, restarts on failure, and participates in [fleet auto-update](/docs/watcher-releases). Foreground `data-hub-watcher watch` is for quick checks and non-Windows hosts.

## Install the service extra [#install-the-service-extra]

The service depends on `pywin32`, which ships in the `windows-service` extra. The [default install](/docs/install-the-watcher#install) already includes it. If you installed without it, add it now:

```sh
uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]"
```

Run [`data-hub-watcher init`](/docs/install-the-watcher#configure) first if you have not configured the watcher yet. The service uses the same `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` and per-environment `.env` file.

## Install and start [#install-and-start]

From an **Administrator** terminal:

```sh
data-hub-watcher service install
data-hub-watcher service start
```

`service install` registers delayed auto-start (so it does not race the network stack at boot), configures restart-on-failure recovery, and registers the `DataHubWatcherUpgrade` Scheduled Task used by the auto-updater.

<Callout type="warn">
  The Windows auto-update path requires that `service install` (or `service reinstall`) has been run from an Administrator shell at least once. Fleet PCs upgrading into an auto-update-capable build for the first time need a one-time `service reinstall` to pick up the task.
</Callout>

## Lifecycle commands [#lifecycle-commands]

| Command                              | What it does                                  |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `data-hub-watcher service install`   | Register the service                          |
| `data-hub-watcher service start`     | Start the service                             |
| `data-hub-watcher service stop`      | Stop the service                              |
| `data-hub-watcher service status`    | Show whether the service is running           |
| `data-hub-watcher service uninstall` | Remove the service                            |
| `data-hub-watcher service reinstall` | Stop, uninstall, install, and start in one go |

`service reinstall` is the right command after an out-of-band wheel swap (for example a manual `uv tool install -U` from an Administrator shell). Stop and uninstall are best-effort, so it works even if the service is already gone.

With watcher 1.4.2 and later, `service stop` finishes within about 25 seconds once the watcher is running, even when Data Hub doesn’t answer. It can take longer while the watcher is still starting. Before watcher 1.4.3 it scanned the whole watch folder first, which takes minutes on a large folder. From 1.4.3 a stop ends the scan at its next file, and the files it hadn’t reached are scanned at the next start. The watcher still syncs its config and sends its first heartbeat before it looks for a stop, so a stop that arrives then waits for Data Hub to answer each request, or for each request to time out after 35 seconds. It can also take longer while the watcher applies a config change from Data Hub, which waits up to 2 minutes for uploads to finish. Once the stop begins, the watcher starts no new file or part. A part already on its way gets up to 15 seconds to arrive. In the last 10 seconds, the watcher sends its `watcher_stopped` event and then its final heartbeat, so it shows as **Stopped** when Data Hub answers.

A file that the watcher had to cut off isn’t lost. When the instrument uploads automatically, the watcher uploads that file again the next time it starts. A file that someone requested with **Upload** is different: `service stop` cancels the requests, so request the file again. A restart of the PC and the stop of an automatic update keep them queued, as [When the PC restarts or shuts down](#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down) describes. See also [Request uploads](/docs/manage-watchers#request-uploads).

`service install` and `service reinstall` accept `--env-path PATH` to override which `.env` file the service loads (defaults to `~/.data-hub/.env.<environment>`).

## When the PC restarts or shuts down [#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down]

With watcher 1.4.1 and later, restarting the PC, or a full shutdown, stops the service the way `service stop` does. The watcher sends a final heartbeat, so it shows as **Stopped** on its page and the instrument reads **Restarting**, and it records a `watcher_stopped` event whose message reads "Service stopped: Windows is shutting down", so you can tell a restart from a `service stop`. On the watcher’s **Activity** tab the event reads “Service stopped because Windows is restarting or shutting down”. The service starts again at boot, as before. `watcher.log` and the Windows Application log both have the line `Data Hub Watcher stopping: Windows is shutting down`.

Files that someone requested with **Upload** stay requested across a restart, and the watcher uploads them once the service is running again. If the PC stays down and no heartbeat arrives for about 15 minutes, Data Hub cancels the requests, and you request the files again. The watcher shows **Stopped** and the instrument reads **Restarting** until then. After that the watcher shows **Unresponsive** and the instrument reads **Offline**, and 30 minutes later the instrument’s subscribers are notified (see [When an instrument goes offline](/docs/configure-notifications#instrument-offline)). A PC that is shut down every night therefore sends an alert each night. Hover over the watcher’s badge on its page to see the time. Stopping the service yourself, with `service stop`, cancels them at once, and the instrument reads **Offline** with the notice “Uploads from this instrument are paused”. See [Request uploads](/docs/manage-watchers#request-uploads).

The same goes for the stop of an automatic update (watcher 1.4.2 and later). The final heartbeat says the stop is for an update, so the watcher shows as **Stopped** and the instrument reads **Restarting**, files someone requested with **Upload** stay requested, and the watcher uploads them once the service is running again on the new version. If no heartbeat arrives for about 15 minutes, Data Hub cancels the requests and the watcher shows as **Unresponsive**. When you update by hand with `data-hub-watcher self-update`, the service stops without that mark, so Data Hub cancels the requests at once, as it does for `service stop`.

Windows waits 10 seconds for a service to stop at a restart on Windows 10 version 1703 and later, and longer on older builds. The watcher limits its own stop to about 8 seconds either way. That is enough for the final heartbeat when Data Hub answers. A file that is still uploading is cut off, not waited for, and the watcher uploads it again after the restart. See [An upload was cut off by a restart or an update](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#an-upload-was-cut-off-by-a-restart-or-an-update).

If Data Hub can’t be reached, or the stop is cut off for another reason, the final heartbeat doesn’t arrive and the service ends with no `stopped` status. If the PC then stays down for more than five minutes, the watcher shows as **Unresponsive** until the service starts again. With watcher 1.4.3 and later, a `watcher_stopped` event that was queued but not sent is recorded once the service starts again, with the time of the stop.

Windows 10 and 11 turn on Fast Startup by default. With it, **Shut down** in the Start menu doesn’t stop the service: Windows saves its state and the service carries on from it at the next start, so no final heartbeat is sent and no `watcher_stopped` event is recorded. **Restart** always stops the service, and so does a shutdown with Fast Startup turned off.

Watchers older than 1.4.1 don’t ask Windows to tell them about a restart, so a restart ends them with no final heartbeat and no `watcher_stopped` event. Updating to 1.4.1 is enough: the service tells Windows what it handles each time it runs, so no `service reinstall` is needed.

## When the watcher is deregistered [#when-the-watcher-is-deregistered]

With watcher 1.4.3 and later, the service stops about three minutes after someone deregisters its watcher or retires its instrument. It stays stopped. The service exits cleanly, so the restart-on-failure recovery doesn’t start it again.

The error is in `watcher.log` and in the Application event log: `This watcher was deregistered on Data Hub, so its registration no longer exists. Run 'data-hub-watcher init' to register it again.` The service sends no `watcher_stopped` event and no final heartbeat, because Data Hub would refuse both.

Starting the service again, including at boot, checks the registration first. If the watcher is still deregistered, the start logs the same error and the service stops with an error. Windows then tries again, after about one minute and then about two minutes, and after that leaves the service stopped. Those are the two retries Windows allows when the service hasn’t failed in the last 24 hours. A service that failed earlier that day gets fewer.

To use the PC again, run `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC. If the instrument was retired, an admin has to reactivate it first, because `init` is refused for a retired instrument (see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument#reactivate)). Then run `data-hub-watcher service start` from an Administrator terminal. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#the-watcher-was-deregistered).

## Do not run `watch` alongside the service [#do-not-run-watch-alongside-the-service]

Running `data-hub-watcher watch` interactively while the service is also running is not supported: both processes would race on the same log file and watch directory. Stop the service first if you need the CLI for debugging:

```powershell
data-hub-watcher service stop
data-hub-watcher --verbose watch
data-hub-watcher service start
```

## Where the service writes logs [#where-the-service-writes-logs]

The service and the CLI share one rotating log:

* `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\watcher.log`

A separate `service-bootstrap.log` next to it captures crashes before the service control dispatcher takes over (missing `pywin32`, moved venv, corrupt install). To turn on debug logging without a reinstall, add `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` to the env file the service loads and restart the service (watcher 1.4.2 and later).

pages.title: Configure run detection and uploads
pages.description: Choose how the watcher groups files into runs, when files are ready to upload, and whether uploads are automatic or approved.
pages.markdown:
# Configure run detection and uploads (/docs/configure-run-detection)



**For:** Lab operators

Tune three behaviors that decide what becomes a run and when bytes leave the instrument PC: run detection, stability period, and upload mode. Field-by-field schema lives in [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference); this page is the intent guide.

Admins can change these from the web app with watcher 1.4.0 and later: on the **Settings** tab of the instrument’s watcher page. See [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). On the PC, set them during `data-hub-watcher init`, with `data-hub-watcher config edit`, or by editing `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` then syncing.

## Group files into runs [#group-files-into-runs]

A **run** is one acquisition: a logical group of files the watcher reports together. **Run detection** maps each file’s path (relative to the watch directory) to a run ID.

Common choices:

* **Prefix from filename**: a regex capture, for example everything before the first underscore so `RUN001_data.csv` → `RUN001`
* **One subdirectory per run**: each folder under the watch directory is its own run, so `RUN001/data.csv` → `RUN001`

Presets and custom regex options are listed under [Run detection](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection). Set `recursive: true` when files live in subfolders; otherwise only the top level is watched.

When a run gathers files from several folders, two files can share a name, such as a `run.json` in each capture folder. Watcher 1.1.0 and later keep every copy and add a short tag to the later names, such as `sample~3f9a1c2b.tif`. Older watchers kept only the first; see [Files with the same name were skipped](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#files-with-the-same-name-were-skipped).

If files appear on disk but never become runs, check for `pattern_mismatch` events on the watcher’s **Activity** tab and run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run`.

## Wait until writes finish [#wait-until-writes-finish]

**Stability period** is how many seconds a file must keep the same size and modification time before the watcher treats it as fully written. Default is 5 seconds (allowed range 1–300). Raise it for instruments that write large files slowly.

A file that keeps changing past `max_stability_wait_seconds` (default 300, or 5 minutes) is abandoned with a `stability_timeout` error event. Raise that cap for instruments whose writes take longer; it must be at least the stability period.

A file that the instrument keeps open after its last write can look finished while the watcher still can’t read it. The watcher’s **Activity** tab shows one **File not ready** event for each such file, saying the watcher can’t read it yet and will try again, and shows another for it each time the watcher starts or its config changes. It tries the file again every minute for as long as it takes, and uploads it once the instrument lets go. A file someone requests with **Upload** on the run page stays requested in the meantime. Watcher 1.4.2 and later do this. Older watchers try such a file again only at the next start, and cancel a request for it after three tries.

## Choose auto or manual upload [#choose-auto-or-manual-upload]

| Mode       | Behavior                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **auto**   | Upload as soon as a file is detected and stable. With watcher 1.2.1 and later, the watcher also picks up files someone requests with **Upload** on the run page, and retries uploads that a restart cut off. |
| **manual** | Report the run, but wait for server approval before uploading bytes. The watcher checks the upload queue once a minute.                                                                                      |

Use manual mode when someone must approve which files leave the instrument PC. Anyone signed in can approve files from the run page, and an instrument in manual mode carries a note beside its file patterns saying files upload when someone requests them; see [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads).

## Existing files on first setup [#existing-files-on-first-setup]

`initial_scan` controls the backlog already in the watch directory when an environment is first entered:

* **`production` default**: upload the backlog (`full`)
* **`staging` / `preview` default**: record a baseline and skip existing files (`new-only`)

Override in config when you need the other behavior. Details: [Initial scan](/docs/configuration-reference#initial-scan).

pages.title: Manage the watcher fleet
pages.description: Open an instrument’s watcher page, monitor watcher health, list every watcher, change a watcher’s settings, deregister watchers, and approve or request uploads.
pages.markdown: # Manage the watcher fleet (/docs/manage-watchers) **For:** Administrators Each instrument’s watcher has its own page, under the instrument, with the watcher’s activity, health, and settings. **Settings → Watchers** lists every watcher in one table, below the form that rolls out new versions. Cutting releases and advertising versions is separate: [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases). Members can open a watcher’s page too, but only to read it. Only admins see the settings form, **Restore**, **Deregister**, and **Settings → Watchers**. What scientists see about an instrument, the status badge and its notices, is in [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive). ## Open a watcher’s page [#the-watcher-page] The watcher is part of its instrument, so its page lives at `/instruments//watcher`. To open it: * Select the status badge beside the instrument’s name * Choose **Watcher** from the three-dot menu on the instrument page, or from a row’s menu on **Instruments** * Select **See details** in a notice on an instrument page or a run page * Select an instrument in the list under **Settings → Watchers** The heading reads **Watcher for** and the instrument’s name, with the watcher’s [status badge](/docs/concepts#watcher-status) beside it. Under it, a summary shows: * **Computer**: the name of the instrument PC * **Operating system** * **Version**: followed by **Up to date** when it matches the **Latest version** under **Settings → Watchers**, or **Update available** and the latest version when it is lower * **Last heartbeat**: how long ago, with the exact time when you hover over it * **Upload mode**: **Automatic** or **Manual** When another active watcher reports the same computer name, compared without regard to capital letters as Windows does, the summary adds a line naming the other instrument or instruments. It says that restarting the computer affects them too, because one PC can run several watchers and restarting it takes every instrument on it offline. Deregistered watchers don’t count. Below the summary, links switch between **Activity**, **Health**, and **Settings**. They are separate addresses, so you can share a link to one: `/watcher` is **Activity**, `/watcher/health` is **Health**, and `/watcher/settings` is **Settings**. ### Past watchers [#past-watchers] An instrument has at most one active watcher, but it keeps every watcher it has had. When it has had more than one, a button at the top of the summary, **Viewing** and a computer name, opens a list of them, newest first. Each entry shows the computer, **Current** or its dates, and who deregistered it. A past watcher opens read-only. Its badge reads **Deregistered**, a notice explains that it is a past watcher and links back to the current one, and every tab shows that watcher’s own events, heartbeats, and settings history. The address ends in `?watcher=` and the watcher’s ID. A watcher ID from another instrument returns a not-found page. When an instrument has no current watcher, because its watcher was deregistered or the instrument was retired, `/watcher` opens on its most recent past watcher with that notice. Admins also see **Connect a new watcher**, which opens [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). An instrument that never had a watcher shows “No watcher has connected yet.” ### Links from before the move [#old-links] Links to the old watcher pages still work. `/watchers/` goes to the instrument’s watcher page, on the matching tab: `?tab=logs` opens **Activity**, `?tab=status` opens **Health**, and `?tab=configuration` opens **Settings**. A deregistered watcher opens as a past watcher. `/watchers` goes to **Settings → Watchers** for admins, on its **Deregistered** tab if the link asked for it, and to **Instruments** for members. ## Monitor watcher health [#monitor-watcher-health] Each watcher sends a [heartbeat](/docs/concepts#heartbeat) every 60 seconds with version, instrument, watch directory, upload mode, activity counters, and uptime. ### Status [#watcher-status-badge] The badge beside the page heading, and in the **Status** column of **Settings → Watchers**, shows the watcher’s state: * **Online**: a heartbeat arrived in the last 5 minutes * **Waiting: folder not found**: running, but its watch folder is missing, or went missing while it ran. Hover over the badge to see which folder * **Unresponsive**: no heartbeat for more than 5 minutes, or more than 15 for a watcher that stopped for a Windows restart, a shutdown, or an automatic update * **Stopped**: shut down cleanly. A stop you chose stays **Stopped** until the watcher starts again, and a stop for a Windows restart, a shutdown, or an automatic update turns **Unresponsive** after 15 minutes * **Registered**: no first heartbeat yet * **Deregistered**: a past watcher See [Watcher status](/docs/concepts#watcher-status). The instrument’s own badge, **Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, or **Offline**, is a simpler summary of the same state, built for the people who use the instrument; see [Instrument status](/docs/concepts#instrument-status). ### Activity [#activity] **Activity** is the watcher’s event log. The heading shows how many events fall in the date range, which starts at **Last 7 days**. Use the **Event type** filter and the date range picker to narrow it. The page shows the first 20 events, and **Show more** loads more. Each event is a row with a label, a plain message, and when it happened. Run IDs in a message link to the run. Select a row to expand it. The expanded row shows details such as the file’s size, the run, and the number of upload parts, with the exact time. Admins also see the raw event, as the watcher sent it, which is the primary tool for remote diagnosis. Members see the plain version only. The labels are **Started**, **Stopped**, **File uploaded**, **Upload failed**, **Run reported**, **Settings synced**, **Error**, **Update started**, **Update finished**, **Update failed**, **Uploads cancelled**, and **Couldn’t upload**. Some events get a more specific label, such as **Missed heartbeat** for an error that says the watcher checked in again after missing some, or **File not ready**, for a file that can’t be read yet, which the watcher tries again. Choosing **Upload failed** in the event type filter leaves out **File not ready** events, because those files haven’t failed. An event of any other type gets a label written from its name. The raw event keeps the type names the docs and the API use, such as `watcher_started`, `run_reported`, `file_uploaded`, `update_*`, and `error` with a `details.kind` discriminator. Data Hub adds `upload_requests_cancelled`, shown as **Uploads cancelled**, when someone deletes a run that has requested uploads. It adds `uploads_failed`, shown as **Couldn’t upload**, when watcher 1.4.5 or later reports files it gave up on: one event per run and reason, such as “Couldn’t upload 129 files in run X: folder no longer on the instrument PC”. The files read **Upload failed**; see [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). Older watchers log a “Queued file missing” and a “Gave up uploading” error for each file instead. From watcher 1.3.0, a `file_uploaded` event reports `size_bytes`, `part_count`, `prep_seconds` (hashing the file and requesting its upload link), and `upload_seconds` (sending the file to storage). Divide `size_bytes` by `upload_seconds` to get the upload speed. Events are the primary remote-diagnosis tool. For operator-side symptoms, see [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher). ### Health [#health] **Health** shows the last 7 days unless you pick another range, up to 31 days. It loads its heartbeat history only when you open it. It has three parts: * Four counts: **Files uploaded**, **Upload failures**, **Restarts** (with the reason, for example “All for automatic updates”), and **Missed heartbeats** (with how long each took to recover). A missed heartbeat is an error event that says the watcher checked in again after missing some * A bar chart of files uploaded per day * **Connectivity**, a grid with one row for each day and one block for each 30 minutes, in your time zone, which the caption names. Green is checked in, gray is restarted for an update, amber is a missed heartbeat that recovered, red is unresponsive, and light gray is no data yet. A block that holds a heartbeat but went quiet for a long stretch with nothing to explain it, such as an outage that is still going, is red too. On a day the clocks change, a block for a half hour that didn’t happen is light gray. Hover over a block to see what happened and when A watcher that shows amber blocks every few hours, or red blocks in the middle of the night, points at the PC or its network rather than at Data Hub. ## See every watcher at once [#all-watchers] **Settings → Watchers**, which only admins see, has the release form from [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases) at the top and the list of **All watchers** below it. There is one watcher per instrument. The heading carries a rollout pill, “14 out of 16 on the latest version” for example. It is green when every watcher runs the latest version or a newer one, and amber otherwise, so you can watch a release catch up. The **Active** tab has one row for each watcher: * **Instrument**: opens the watcher’s page * **Computer**: sortable, with a stacked-layers icon when other active watchers share it. Hover over the icon, or focus it with the keyboard, to see how many watchers run on that computer and which instruments * **Version** * **Status**: the watcher’s [status badge](#watcher-status-badge) * **Settings**: **Change pending**, **Change rejected**, **Edited on PC, restart pending**, or a dash when there is nothing to report; see [Change a watcher’s settings](#change-a-watchers-config) * **Last heartbeat** * A three-dot menu with **Deregister** The **Deregistered** tab lists past watchers, with the **Instrument**, **Computer**, **Last version**, the date it was **Deregistered on**, and who it was **Deregistered by**. ## Change a watcher’s settings [#change-a-watchers-config] Admins can change a watcher’s settings from the web app, without visiting the instrument PC. This needs watcher 1.4.0 or later. For older watchers the form is turned off with a note to update the watcher. Open the watcher’s page and choose the **Settings** tab. It shows: * **Current settings**: what the watcher is running now, as it last reported. Admins get an **Edit** button here, which opens the form in a dialog with **Save change** and **Preview with recent files**. Saving closes the dialog. * **History**: every change, with who made it and when * **Raw config file (YAML)**, folded away at the bottom You can change: * **Watch folder**: any folder on the instrument PC * **File patterns** * **How files become runs**: a preset or your own pattern, and whether to include subfolders * **Upload mode**, **Parallel uploads**, **Stability period**, and **Max stability wait** The form checks each value as you type. **Preview with recent files** shows which of the instrument’s recent files the new patterns match and the run ID each would get. It only covers files Data Hub already knows about, so files on the PC that never matched a pattern don’t appear. After you save: 1. A **Change pending** notice appears at the top of the tab. 2. Within about a minute, the watcher’s next heartbeat tells it a change is waiting. The watcher fetches it. 3. The watcher checks the change, including that the new folder exists and can be read. If a check fails, it keeps its current settings and a **Change rejected** notice gives the reason, both on the **Settings** tab and as an `error` event. 4. Otherwise it saves the new settings to `config.yaml`, waits up to two minutes for the uploads it’s sending, and restarts its watching with the new settings. The change shows as **Applied**, and **Current settings** updates. A file that hadn’t finished uploading, such as a large file partway through, uploads again from the start after the change, unless the change moved the watch folder or switched to manual uploads. If the new settings match more files, the watcher reports files that are already on the PC as detected, but doesn’t upload them. To upload them, use **Upload** on the run page; see [Request uploads](#request-uploads). New files after the change follow the upload mode. If the watcher is offline, the change waits and is applied when the watcher next starts. If someone also edited `config.yaml` on the PC while it was offline, the newer of the two edits wins and the other stays in the history. The same form also opens from the notice on an instrument page that says Data Hub can’t find the watch folder: **Change folder** opens **Settings** with the form already open and the **Watch folder** field selected. See [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive). ### Edits made on the PC [#edits-on-the-pc] An edit made on the PC while the watcher is running, such as with `data-hub-watcher config edit`, is saved to `config.yaml` and recorded in the history at once, as **Applied**. The watcher reads `config.yaml` only when it starts, though, so it keeps running its previous settings until it restarts. Until then the **Settings** tab shows **Edited on PC — restart pending**, and **Settings → Watchers** shows **Edited on PC, restart pending**. With watcher 1.4.0 and later, **Current settings** shows what the watcher is running, from the revision it reports in its heartbeat. ### History and restore [#config-history] The **History** card records every change, whether it came from Data Hub or from the config file on the PC (such as `data-hub-watcher config edit`). Each entry has its revision number, its state, who made it, or **From the instrument PC**, when, and a one-line summary of what changed. To go back to an earlier version, click **Restore** on it. That saves its settings as a new change, and never edits the history. When two admins edit the same watcher at once, the second save is refused with a message to reload, so neither overwrites the other unseen. Members see the same cards, with the current settings, any notice, and the history, but no form and no **Restore**. A line with a lock icon says “Only admins can change watcher settings.” ### Change settings with the API or an AI assistant [#change-settings-with-the-api-or-an-ai-assistant] * **API**: `POST /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId/config-revisions` with `base_revision` and the full `settings`. Signed-in callers must be admins; tokens must list `watchers:admin` explicitly (legacy `*` and `watchers:write` tokens are refused). `GET /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId/config-revisions` lists the history. See the [generated API docs](/docs/api). * **MCP**: the `update_watcher_config` tool, for admins. It changes only the settings you name. The assistant shows you the change and asks you to confirm before it saves. ## Deregister a watcher [#deregister-a-watcher] Each instrument can have at most one active watcher. Deregister the old one when a PC is reimaged or replaced, or to clear “instrument already has an active watcher” on a new install. * **Web app**: open the watcher’s page, choose **Deregister** from its three-dot menu, or choose **Deregister** from the watcher’s row menu in **Settings → Watchers**. The dialog asks you to stop the watcher service on the PC first * **API**: `DELETE /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId` (requires `watchers:admin`) Deregistration is a soft-delete: heartbeats, events, and runs stay with the instrument, under its past watchers and on the **Deregistered** tab of **Settings → Watchers**. The instrument’s badge reads **Offline** until a new watcher registers, and its page says when the watcher was deregistered and by whom. A watcher removed through the API with a token shows that token’s name as the one that removed it. A running watcher that is deregistered stops by itself within about three minutes (watcher 1.4.3 and later). It doesn’t come back on its own. The Windows service isn’t restarted either, and a start is refused. To use the PC again, run `data-hub-watcher init` on the instrument PC. Older watchers keep running and getting errors until someone stops them on the PC. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#the-watcher-was-deregistered). Retiring an instrument also deregisters its watcher automatically; see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument). `init` is refused for a retired instrument, so reactivate it before anyone runs `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC again (see [Reactivate](/docs/retire-an-instrument#reactivate)). You don’t need to deregister a watcher just because its token was revoked. Re-running `data-hub-watcher init` with a new token takes over the existing registration; see [After revoking a token](/docs/manage-tokens#after-revoking-a-token). ## Request uploads [#request-uploads] **Upload** on a run page, or on selected runs in a run list, asks the watcher to send files that are still on the instrument PC. The watcher polls the server’s upload queue once a minute and uploads the files that were requested. * In **manual** upload mode, every file waits in this queue until someone requests it. * In **auto** upload mode, files upload on their own, and the queue covers files that need another try. This works with watcher 1.2.1 and later; older watchers in auto mode never pick up requests, so the file shows **Uploading** and stays that way. The **Upload** buttons on a run page follow the instrument’s badge. They work while it reads **Online** or **Restarting**, and are turned off for **Connecting**, **Offline**, **Pending**, and **Retired**, with the reason beside the button. Data Hub also refuses a request for such an instrument. See [Request an upload](/docs/browse-runs#request-upload). When a watcher stops cleanly and shows as **Stopped**, Data Hub cancels its pending requests and the files go back to `detected`, because nothing is left to upload them. Two stops are the exception, because the watcher is expected back: restarting the instrument PC or a full shutdown (watcher 1.4.1 and later), and a watcher that stops to install an automatic update (watcher 1.4.2 and later). The instrument reads **Restarting**, and the requests stay queued for the watcher to upload once it is running again. Data Hub cancels them only if no heartbeat arrives for about 15 minutes. At that point the watcher shows as **Unresponsive** instead of **Stopped**, and the instrument reads **Offline**. See [When the PC restarts or shuts down](/docs/windows-service#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down). Deleting a run also cancels the pending requests for that run’s files, and the files go back to `detected`. Data Hub records an `upload_requests_cancelled` event on the instrument’s watcher with the run and the number of files, and you can filter **Activity** by **Uploads cancelled** to find it. That event covers only cancellations caused by deleting a run. The other cancellations in this section, such as a watcher stopping or being removed or a change of watch folder, still show under their own event types. Restoring the run doesn’t bring the requests back, so request the uploads again. Other runs on the instrument keep their requests. ## Approving manual uploads [#approving-manual-uploads] For instruments in [manual upload mode](/docs/concepts#upload-mode), the watcher reports runs but waits for server approval before uploading file bytes. The instrument’s page carries a note, “Files upload when someone requests them,” beside its file patterns. Approve a file with **Upload**, or choose **Dismiss** to tell the watcher not to upload it. To act on several files at once, select them in the files table and use the bar that appears. Safeguards that keep the queue healthy: * Changing an instrument’s watch folder, from the web app or on the PC, reverts pending upload requests to `detected` so stale paths drain instead of erroring * A queued file that keeps failing (missing on disk or failing to upload) is retried on at most three polls, then cancelled server-side, and a file requested again gets three new tries (before watcher 1.4.3, a request made right after the cancellation was cancelled at once)

pages.title: Roll out watcher releases
pages.description: Publish watcher versions to PyPI, advertise them per environment, set a minimum version, force mandatory updates, roll the fleet back, and see what each version adds.
pages.markdown: # Roll out watcher releases (/docs/watcher-releases) **For:** Administrators Lab PCs upgrade themselves toward the version you advertise per environment. You control that from **Settings → Watchers**, which also lists every watcher with its version, so you can watch a release catch up. How an individual PC installs or runs `self-update` is in [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher). ## How fleet upgrades reach a PC [#how-fleet-upgrades-reach-a-pc] The in-process updater runs from the heartbeat tick on every platform (not only Windows services). Roughly once an hour the watcher: 1. Asks the server for the latest version and compares it to its own 2. Upgrades only if a newer version is available, no files have uploaded for several heartbeats, and no run was reported recently (the activity-window guard). Releases flagged **mandatory** skip this guard 3. Installs the new wheel and restarts into it (Windows services restart via failure-actions policy) 4. Emits `update_started`, then `update_succeeded` or `update_failed`, which a watcher’s **Activity** tab shows as **Update started**, **Update finished**, or **Update failed** Auto-update is disabled in the `preview` environment so pull-request preview deployments cannot push code to lab PCs. ## Cut a new release [#cut-a-new-release] Releases are tag-driven and publish from a `production` commit. Bump the version in `watcher/pyproject.toml` and merge through `staging` to `production`. Tag and push from `production`: ```sh git checkout production && git pull git tag watcher-v1.3.0 && git push origin watcher-v1.3.0 ``` Approve the `pypi` deployment under **Actions → Publish watcher** in GitHub. In **Settings → Watchers**, pick the new version under **Latest version**. The list comes straight from PyPI, so a release shows up as soon as PyPI publishes it. If PyPI can’t be reached, the field accepts a typed version instead. Each environment has its own database, so set `staging` and `production` separately to roll the fleet gradually. Always tag → publish → verify on PyPI → save. Saving **Latest version** before the wheel is live triggers a wave of `update_failed` events across the fleet. ## Release settings [#release-config-fields] | Field | Purpose | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Latest version** | The version watchers upgrade to. Leave it blank to pause self-updates. | | **Minimum supported version** | Optional. A watcher older than this has its heartbeats rejected with `426 Upgrade Required`, so it shows as unresponsive until it updates. It still checks for updates every hour, so it upgrades itself as long as **Latest version** is newer. Leave it blank for no minimum. | | **Mandatory update** | Skips the activity-window guard; see below. Has no effect while **Latest version** is blank. | ## Watch the rollout [#watch-the-rollout] Below the release form, **All watchers** has a pill that reads “*N* out of *M* on the latest version”. It is green when every active watcher runs that version or a newer one, and amber while some are behind. The **Version** column shows each watcher’s version. A watcher’s own page says **Up to date**, or **Update available** with the latest version, beside its version. After a rollback, a watcher still on a newer build counts as current, so the pill stays green while it hasn’t moved to the older version you set. Check the **Version** column to see which watchers have. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#all-watchers). ## Mandatory updates [#mandatory-updates] Toggling **Mandatory update** skips the activity-window guard and fires the upgrade on the next hourly check. The server still compares the running version to **Latest version**, so a correctly pinned PC is not forced past its pin. Use sparingly: a forced upgrade mid-acquisition can lose data. Reserve it for security fixes, wire-protocol breaks, or cases where leaving the bad version running is worse than restarting in flight. ## Roll back [#roll-back] Rollback is another release: set **Latest version** back to the older tag for the affected environment(s), turn **Mandatory update** on if you need to bypass the activity-window guard, and wait for the next hourly tick. Turn **Mandatory update** off once the fleet converges. The older wheel remains on PyPI; it is no longer advertised. If **Minimum supported version** is set above the version you roll back to, lower it first. Otherwise the rolled-back watchers can’t check in. ## What each version adds [#what-each-version-adds] Some Data Hub features need a minimum watcher version. Set **Latest version** to at least the version below to turn a feature on across the fleet. | Version | What it adds | | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | 1.4.5 | A file the watcher gives up on is marked **Upload failed**, with the reason, instead of quietly going back to not uploaded: a requested file that isn’t on the instrument PC, for example because its run folder was renamed or moved, or one whose upload failed three times. Data Hub records one event per run and reason, where older watchers record events for every file. In auto mode, a file whose upload fails is marked **Upload failed** at once, and the watcher still tries it again the next time it starts. Files an auto-mode watcher is about to upload show as **Waiting to upload**, and files it reports without uploading, such as the ones already on the PC after a change that matches more files, as **Not uploaded**. With older watchers, auto-mode files show as **Not uploaded** until they upload, and a file the watcher gives up on goes back to not uploaded with no reason. | | 1.4.3 | A watcher whose watch folder disappears while it runs, for example when a network drive drops, goes back to waiting, as it does when the folder is missing at startup, and starts watching again once the folder is back. A share that has stopped answering no longer freezes the watcher, and files waiting to upload aren’t dropped while the folder is gone. A stop while the watcher is starting up, including during the scan of a large folder, ends cleanly with the `stopped` status and event, for `data-hub-watcher watch` and for the Windows service. A watcher whose registration was deleted on Data Hub stops after Data Hub has said so on three heartbeats in a row, about 3 minutes, and says to run `data-hub-watcher init`. `data-hub-watcher watch` exits with code 3, the Windows service stays stopped, and starting such a watcher is refused with the same message. Any other error, such as Data Hub having no record of the watcher, doesn’t stop it. Heartbeat counts are no longer lost when a heartbeat fails or while one is being sent. Events that haven’t been sent yet are kept across a restart or a crash and across a Data Hub outage, and sent afterwards. Events that Data Hub refuses, or fails to take on three tries in a row, are dropped, and an `events_dropped` event says how many. A file of 100 MB or more that changed while it uploaded is hashed again and uploaded as it is then, instead of failing, and a file requested again right after its request was cancelled gets a fresh set of three tries. A watcher that finds a run deleted on Data Hub records one event for it and leaves the run alone until it restarts, or until Data Hub accepts an upload that someone requested for one of the run’s files, instead of recording an error for every file. Older watchers keep reporting that they are watching when their folder disappears, can end with no `stopped` status when they are stopped during start-up, keep running and uploading after their registration is deleted, lose heartbeat counts and unsent events, fail the upload of a file of 100 MB or more that changed while it uploaded, cancel a request made right after a cancellation without trying the file, and record an error for every file of a deleted run. | | 1.4.2 | Once the watcher is running, a stop finishes within about 25 seconds, even when Data Hub isn’t answering. The watcher sends its events before its final heartbeat, and starts no new part or file once a stop is requested. A watcher that stops to install an automatic update tells Data Hub why, so files someone asked for with **Upload** stay requested while it comes back, and the Windows service hands an upgrade to its worker only once. The Windows service also records a config or env file it can’t load in `watcher.log`, and honors `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL` from its env file. A file the instrument keeps open after its last write is uploaded once the instrument lets go of it: the watcher tries it again every minute until it can be read, and a request for it from the run page stays requested. Older watchers try such a file again only at the next start, and cancel a request for it after three tries. | | 1.4.1 | Restarting a Windows instrument PC stops the watcher service cleanly. The watcher sends a final heartbeat, so it shows as **Stopped**, and files someone asked for with **Upload** stay requested and upload once the PC is back. Data Hub cancels those requests if the watcher isn’t back within about 15 minutes; see [When the PC restarts or shuts down](/docs/windows-service#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down). Older watchers are ended by a restart without recording a stop. In auto mode, the files of a run reported just before a restart, a power cut or a crash upload after the next start; older watchers can leave them showing **Waiting to upload**, and [they can be uploaded from the run page](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#a-file-stays-pending-after-the-watcher-restarted). A run whose ID contains `#`, `?` or another character with a special meaning in a web address gets its own files; older watchers send them to another run or don't upload them. | | 1.4.0 | Admins can [change the watcher’s config from Data Hub](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). The watcher picks up a saved change within about a minute and applies it, or rejects it and keeps its current settings when a check fails, such as a folder that doesn’t exist. After a change that matches more files, the watcher reports files already on the PC as detected but doesn’t upload them. A watcher whose folder is missing at startup keeps running and shows **Waiting: folder not found**, so the folder can be fixed from Data Hub. Older watchers can only be changed on the instrument PC, and exit at startup when their folder is missing. | | 1.3.0 | A large file uploads several parts at once, and several files requested from the run page upload side by side. Together they stay within the [`instrument.upload_parallelism`](/docs/configuration-reference#field-reference) setting, 4 uploads by default. Older watchers send one part, or one requested file, at a time, so a large file goes no faster than a single connection allows. The watcher asks again for a part’s upload link after a connection error or a server error, instead of failing the file. It still fails the file when Data Hub rejects the request (a 4xx response). The `file_uploaded` event also records the file’s size and how long preparing and sending it took. | | 1.2.2 | A run report that fails because the watcher can’t reach Data Hub, or because Data Hub returns a server error, is retried until it goes through. Older watchers leave the run unreported until another file in the run finishes or the watcher restarts. | | 1.2.1 | **Request upload** works on instruments that upload automatically; older watchers in auto mode leave the file showing **Uploading**. The watcher also retries an automatic upload that didn’t finish, such as one cut off by a restart or an update, the next time it starts. It tries on up to three starts. | | 1.2.0 | Files of 100 MB or more upload in 64 MB parts, and a failed part is retried on its own. Files larger than 5 GB can upload; older watchers are refused for files that large. | | 1.1.0 | When a run gathers files from several folders, files with the same name are all kept instead of only the first. Later copies get a short tag in the name, such as `sample~3f9a1c2b.tif`. Adds the `data-hub-watcher state forget` command. | After upgrading to 1.1.0 or later, files that an older watcher skipped because of a duplicate name aren’t uploaded on their own. To upload them, stop the watcher, run `data-hub-watcher state forget --prefix your_folder_name/` on the instrument PC, and start the watcher again. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#files-with-the-same-name-were-skipped). ## Operator-side failures [#operator-side-failures] If `update_started` is followed by `update_failed`, or auto-update never fires, point operators at [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#auto-update-never-fires) and [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher#manual-update-self-update).

pages.title: Troubleshoot a watcher
pages.description: Fix watcher problems by symptom: will not start, files not detected, uploads stuck, auto-update quiet, and where to find logs.
pages.markdown: # Troubleshoot a watcher (/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher) **For:** Lab operators and admins Find your symptom below. When you are stuck, the [logs](#where-are-the-logs) are the fastest way in. Admins can also inspect events, heartbeats, and settings on the instrument’s watcher page: select the status badge beside the instrument’s name, or choose **Watcher** from its three-dot menu. Members can open that page too, to read it. ## An instrument shows Offline [#instrument-shows-offline] An instrument’s badge reads **Offline** when new files can’t reach Data Hub right now. A notice under the instrument’s name says why, and **See details** opens the watcher’s **Activity** tab. Find the notice below. | Notice | What it means | What to do | | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **New files aren’t being picked up** | The watcher is running but can’t find its watch folder. | Create or reconnect the folder on the PC, or let an admin choose **Change folder**. See [The watcher shows “Waiting: folder not found”](#waiting-folder-not-found). | | **The watcher isn’t checking in** | No heartbeat for 5 minutes, or the watcher didn’t come back within 15 minutes of a restart or an update. The PC may be off, the watcher may have crashed, or the network may be blocking Data Hub. | On the PC, check that the watcher is running (`data-hub-watcher service status` on Windows) and that it can reach Data Hub; see [“Connection error” or “Request timed out”](#connection-error-or-request-timed-out). Its last events are on the **Activity** tab. | | **The watcher never checked in** | The watcher registered but sent no heartbeat within 15 minutes of registering, or of an admin confirming the instrument if that came later. The service may never have started, or the PC can’t reach Data Hub. | Start the watcher on the PC, as in [step 5 of Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument#start-the-watcher-service). If it won’t start, see [The watcher will not start](#the-watcher-will-not-start). If it is running, check that it can reach Data Hub; see [“Connection error” or “Request timed out”](#connection-error-or-request-timed-out). | | **Uploads from this instrument are paused** | Someone stopped the watcher, for example with `data-hub-watcher service stop` or Ctrl+C. | Start it again: `data-hub-watcher service start` on Windows, or `data-hub-watcher watch`. | | **This instrument isn’t connected to a watcher** | The instrument never had a watcher, or its watcher was deregistered, which the notice dates and credits. | Run `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC; see [The watcher stopped and says it was deregistered](#the-watcher-was-deregistered). Admins can follow **Connect a watcher**. | **Restarting** and **Connecting** aren’t problems: each turns **Offline** if it lasts more than 15 minutes. See [The instrument shows Restarting after a restart](#the-instrument-shows-restarting-after-a-restart). Files saved on the PC while an instrument is offline stay there, and the watcher picks them up once it runs again. People who subscribe to the instrument hear about it once the badge has read **Offline** for 30 minutes, in the app and in Slack if they turned that on, with the notice’s reason. They hear again when it’s back **Online**. See [When an instrument goes offline](/docs/configure-notifications#instrument-offline). ## Setup and registration [#setup-and-registration] ### “Instrument is still pending activation” [#instrument-is-still-pending-activation] The instrument was registered but an admin has not confirmed it. Its badge reads **Pending**. Ask an admin to open **Instruments**, click **Confirm…**, pick an instrument type, and choose **Confirm instrument**. See [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments#confirm-a-pending-instrument). ### “Instrument already has an active watcher” [#instrument-already-has-an-active-watcher] Each instrument can have at most one active watcher. An earlier install (often on another PC, or before a reimage) is still registered. The CLI prints the existing watcher id; deregister it before re-running `init`: * **Web app**: open the instrument, select its status badge to open its watcher page, and choose **Deregister** from the ⋮ menu. You can also use the row menu in **Settings → Watchers**. Only admins see those menus. Watcher 1.4.3’s message names a menu that no longer exists; watcher 1.4.4 prints the address of the watcher’s page instead * **API**: `DELETE /api/v1/watchers/` with a bearer token that has `watchers:admin` Deregistration is a soft-delete: the history stays with the instrument as a past watcher, and on the **Deregistered** tab of **Settings → Watchers**. ### `init` rejects my API key [#init-rejects-my-api-key] The wizard rejects values that do not start with `dhub_`, and strips zero-width and non-breaking-space characters that Windows clipboards inject. If a paste keeps failing, pass `--show-key` so you can see what the prompt received. ## The watcher will not start [#the-watcher-will-not-start] * Run `data-hub-watcher config show` to confirm config and environment * Run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run`: it prints the first failing check * Confirm the instrument is `active`, not `pending` * On Windows, if the **service** will not start, see [Windows service](#windows-service) ## The watcher stopped and says it was deregistered [#the-watcher-was-deregistered] Someone deleted the watcher’s registration on Data Hub. This happens when an admin deregisters the watcher in the web app, or retires its instrument (see [Deregister a watcher](/docs/manage-watchers#deregister-a-watcher)). After a deregistration, the instrument reads **Offline** and its notice says its watcher was deregistered. A retired instrument reads **Retired**, with no notice. Watcher 1.4.3 and later stop by themselves when this happens. The watcher logs one error: `This watcher was deregistered on Data Hub, so its registration no longer exists. Run 'data-hub-watcher init' to register it again.` You can find that error in `watcher.log` (see [Where are the logs?](#where-are-the-logs)). On Windows, it is also in the Application event log, and `service status` shows the service as stopped. The watcher waits for three heartbeats in a row that Data Hub answers with its “deregistered” reply. At the usual one-minute interval, that is about three minutes, so one wrong answer can’t stop the watcher. A different error, including Data Hub saying it has no watcher with that ID, doesn’t stop it. Once it has stopped, it uploads nothing and doesn’t come back on its own. Starting it again is refused with the same message. `watch` exits with code 3 when it stops this way, and when it refuses to start. To use the PC again, run `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC. This registers a new watcher for the instrument. If the instrument was retired, `init` is refused until an admin reactivates the instrument (see [Reactivate](/docs/retire-an-instrument#reactivate)). The PC keeps its upload history, so files that were already uploaded aren’t uploaded again. If `init` reports that the instrument already has an active watcher, see [Instrument already has an active watcher](#instrument-already-has-an-active-watcher). On Windows, then run `data-hub-watcher service start` from an Administrator terminal. Watchers older than 1.4.3 don’t stop. They keep running and get errors from Data Hub until someone stops them. ## The watcher shows “Waiting: folder not found” [#waiting-folder-not-found] Watcher 1.4.0 and later start even when the watch folder is missing, for example when a network drive isn’t connected yet or the folder was renamed. The watcher keeps sending heartbeats but watches nothing. Its page shows **Waiting: folder not found**, and the instrument reads **Offline** with the notice “New files aren’t being picked up”. Hover over the watcher’s badge to see which folder it’s looking for; the notice names it too. The watcher checks for the folder again once a minute and starts watching as soon as it appears. To fix it: * Create or reconnect the folder on the PC, or * Point the watcher at the right folder from the web app: an admin chooses **Change folder** in the notice, which opens the watcher’s **Settings** tab with the **Watch folder** field selected; see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config) Watcher 1.4.3 and later also go back to this state when the folder disappears while they run, for example when a network drive drops or the folder is deleted. The watcher notices within a minute, looks again a few seconds later so that a drop of a moment doesn’t count, stops watching, and shows **Waiting: folder not found**. It gives a file that was uploading at that moment up to 10 seconds to finish, cuts it off if it isn’t done, and uploads it again once the folder is back. When the folder returns, the watcher starts watching it again without a restart, and queues a `watcher_started` event that says it resumed. Older watchers exit at startup instead, with an error that the watch directory doesn’t exist. ## A config change shows “Change rejected” [#change-rejected] The watcher checked a change made in the web app and refused it, so it kept its previous settings. The reason shows in a **Change rejected** notice on the watcher’s **Settings** tab and as an `error` event with `details.kind` set to `config_revision_rejected`. The most common reason is a folder that doesn’t exist or can’t be read on the PC. Fix the cause, then save the change again or **Restore** an earlier version from the history. ## “Data Hub can’t read the watcher’s config file” [#config-file-unreadable] The watcher’s **Settings** tab shows this when the `config.yaml` the watcher sent breaks the rules the web app checks, for example a relative watch folder, more than 50 file patterns, or a run detection pattern with Python-only syntax such as `(?P…)`. The notice names each field that needs fixing, by its key in the file. Until it’s fixed, edits made on the PC aren’t recorded in the history, and if Data Hub has no earlier revision of the settings, there are none to edit there. Fix the file on the instrument PC, for example with `data-hub-watcher config edit`. ## A config change stays on “Change pending” [#change-pending] The watcher picks up a change after its next heartbeat, within about a minute. If it stays pending: * Check that the watcher is **Online** on its page. An offline watcher applies the change when it next starts. * Check that the watcher runs 1.4.0 or later. The web app won’t save changes for older watchers. ## The instrument shows Restarting after a restart [#the-instrument-shows-restarting-after-a-restart] When the PC restarts, or the watcher stops to install an automatic update, the instrument’s badge reads **Restarting** for up to 15 minutes, not **Offline**. Nothing is wrong. The watcher checks in once a minute, so it can take up to a minute after the service starts to show as **Online**. Refresh the page after a minute. A new watcher reads **Connecting** until its first check-in, and **Offline**, with the notice “The watcher never checked in”, if none arrives within 15 minutes. If the badge turns **Offline** with the notice “The watcher isn’t checking in”, the watcher didn’t come back. Check that the process is running and see [“Connection error” or “Request timed out”](#connection-error-or-request-timed-out). Older watchers don’t say they are restarting, so they read **Offline** from the moment the PC goes down; see [When the PC restarts or shuts down](/docs/windows-service#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down). ## Heartbeats fail with `426 Upgrade Required` [#heartbeats-fail-with-426-upgrade-required] The watcher is older than the **Minimum supported version** an admin set under **Settings → Watchers**, so the server rejects its heartbeats and it shows as unresponsive. Its instrument reads **Offline**. It keeps checking for updates every hour and upgrades itself if **Latest version** is newer. To upgrade now, run `data-hub-watcher self-update`. See [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#release-config-fields). ## “Connection error” or “Request timed out” [#connection-error-or-request-timed-out] The watcher cannot reach the Data Hub API. Check: * Network connectivity from the instrument PC * Environment in config (`staging`, `production`, or `preview`): `data-hub-watcher config show` * That the API base URL for that environment is reachable ### A run is missing after a connection problem [#a-run-is-missing-after-a-connection-problem] Watcher 1.2.2 and later retry a run report that failed because the watcher couldn’t reach Data Hub, or because Data Hub returned a server error. The first retry comes after 5 seconds. The wait then doubles up to 5 minutes between tries, and the watcher keeps trying every 5 minutes until the report goes through. It needs no new file and no restart, so the run appears on its own once the problem clears. The watcher records one `run_report_failed` event when a run’s report first fails. It doesn’t record another for the same run while it keeps retrying, even if more files in the run finish in the meantime. A failure that isn’t a connection problem or a server error, such as `401 Unauthorized`, is not retried, because it would fail the same way. Each one is recorded, except the refusals of a run that was deleted on Data Hub, which watcher 1.4.3 and later record once per run (see [A run was deleted on Data Hub](#a-run-was-deleted-on-data-hub)). Fix the cause, then restart the watcher. Older watchers try again only when another file in the run finishes or the watcher restarts. Restart the watcher to report the run. ## A run was deleted on Data Hub [#a-run-was-deleted-on-data-hub] A run report or an upload request that fails with `409 Conflict` and a message that starts “This run was deleted on Data Hub” means someone deleted the run. Data Hub refuses a watcher’s report of a deleted run, and its requests to upload the run’s files, and the files in a refused report aren’t added to the run. Watcher 1.4.3 and later record one event for the run, a `run_report_failed` event or an `upload_failed` event, whichever the watcher meets first, and stop reporting the run and uploading its files until the watcher restarts. A restart tries once more, and records one more event if the run is still deleted. After you restore the run, restart the watcher to send its files. A file that someone requests with **Upload** on the run page doesn’t wait for the restart: the watcher asks Data Hub for each requested file, and once Data Hub accepts one, the watcher reports and uploads the run’s new files again. Earlier watchers record one event for each file, and do it again each time they start. After you restore the run, they send its files when another file of the run finishes or the watcher restarts. To stop the errors without restoring the run, move the run’s files out of the watch folder. ## Files are not being detected [#files-are-not-being-detected] * Confirm the watch directory and file patterns. The instrument’s page in the web app shows both, or run `data-hub-watcher config show` on the PC. Admins can change them from the web app; see [Change a watcher’s config](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config) * Check that the instrument saves its files into that folder, not a shared network drive or another folder * Check file patterns. Globs are case-sensitive (`*.csv` does not match `data.CSV`) * If files live in subfolders, set run detection to recursive; see [Configure run detection and uploads](/docs/configure-run-detection) * Run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run` to preview matches * Look for `pattern_mismatch` events on the watcher’s **Activity** tab ## Files are detected but not uploading [#files-are-detected-but-not-uploading] * In **manual** mode, files wait for approval in the upload queue; see [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads) * On the run page, the **Upload** buttons are turned off while the instrument is **Connecting**, **Offline**, **Pending**, or **Retired**, with the reason beside them. Fix the watcher first; see [An instrument shows Offline](#instrument-shows-offline). While the instrument is **Restarting** they stay on, and the request waits for the watcher * Files read **Not uploaded** until someone requests them, or **Waiting to upload** while an auto-mode watcher (1.4.5 and later) is about to send them * A file that reads **Upload failed** is one the watcher gave up on. Hover over its status for the reason; see [A file reads Upload failed](#a-file-reads-upload-failed) * Check the log for `upload_failed` * A `state_write_failed` event in the watcher’s event log means the PC’s disk is full or the watcher’s state file can’t be written. Free up space; the watcher retries on its own and uploads the files once it can write again * A revoked or expired token surfaces as `401 Unauthorized`. Create a new token and re-run `init`; see [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens#after-revoking-a-token) ### A file reads Upload failed [#a-file-reads-upload-failed] Watcher 1.4.5 and later mark a file **Upload failed** when they give up on it, and the watcher’s activity shows one **Couldn’t upload** entry per run and reason. Hover over the file’s status for the reason: * **The folder is no longer on the instrument PC.** The run folder was renamed or moved after the watcher found it. The watcher reports the folder under its new name as a new run, so check for a run with the same start time and a similar name: its files are usually already uploaded, and you can dismiss the old ones. * **The file isn’t on the instrument PC.** The file was moved or deleted. Put it back and choose **Upload**, or choose **Dismiss**. * **The upload kept failing.** Usually a network or storage problem. The message shows the last error. Choose **Upload** to try again once it’s fixed. * **The path is outside the watch folder.** Check the watcher’s **Watch folder** setting. Older watchers put the file back to **Not uploaded** without a reason, and log a “Queued file missing” and a “Gave up uploading” error for each file instead. See [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). ### A requested upload stays on Uploading [#a-requested-upload-stays-on-uploading] On an instrument in **auto** mode, **Request upload** needs watcher 1.2.1 or later. Older watchers in auto mode never read the upload queue, so the file shows **Uploading** and never arrives. Update the watcher; see [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds). ### Files larger than 5 GB don’t upload [#files-larger-than-5-gb-dont-upload] Watchers older than 1.2.0 can’t upload files larger than 5 GB, and Data Hub refuses the upload instead of letting it fail partway. Update the watcher to 1.2.0 or later, which uploads large files in parts. ### An upload was cut off by a restart or an update [#an-upload-was-cut-off-by-a-restart-or-an-update] Watcher 1.2.1 and later retry an automatic upload that didn’t finish the next time the watcher starts, on up to three starts. Two events tell you when it stops trying: * `upload_retries_exhausted`: the upload still failed after three starts. Choose **Upload** on the file’s run page to try again. * `pending_upload_missing`: the file was no longer on disk when the watcher started, so there was nothing to retry. From watcher 1.4.5, the file reads **Upload failed** as soon as an automatic upload fails, with the reason on the file instead of these events, and the watcher still retries it on its next starts. Older watchers don’t retry; use **Upload** on the run page instead. ### A file stays on Waiting to upload after the watcher restarted [#a-file-stays-pending-after-the-watcher-restarted] Watchers before 1.4.1 could lose track of a file in an automatic upload when the watcher stopped without shutting down cleanly, such as after a reboot, a power cut, or a crash, just after it reported the run. The run is in Data Hub, but the file reads **Not uploaded** and nothing uploads it, because after the restart the watcher treats the file as already handled. Watcher 1.4.1 and later record a run and its files on the PC together, so a restart like that doesn’t leave a file behind. Updating doesn’t pick up files that an older watcher already lost this way. Ask for them from the run page: If the watcher is older than 1.2.1, update it first.
