Older watchers in auto mode ignore upload requests; see [A requested upload stays on Uploading](#a-requested-upload-stays-on-uploading). Open the run, select the files that read **Not uploaded**, and choose **Upload**. To ask for the files of several runs at once, select the runs in the run list and choose **Upload**. See [Request an upload](/docs/browse-runs#request-upload). The watcher picks up the request within a minute and uploads the files that are still on the instrument PC. ### Files with the same name were skipped [#files-with-the-same-name-were-skipped] When a run gathers files from several folders, watchers older than 1.1.0 uploaded only the first file with a given name and skipped the rest. Watcher 1.1.0 and later keep every copy, adding a short tag to later names. To upload files an older watcher skipped: Update the watcher to 1.1.0 or later. Stop the watcher (`data-hub-watcher service stop`, or `Ctrl+C` in the foreground). Run `data-hub-watcher state forget --prefix your_folder_name/` on the instrument PC, where `your_folder_name/` is the folder under the watch directory that held the skipped files. Start the watcher again. It reports the files in that folder again and uploads the ones Data Hub doesn’t have. A run that was deleted on Data Hub refuses its files instead. See [A run was deleted on Data Hub](#a-run-was-deleted-on-data-hub). ## Auto-update never fires [#auto-update-never-fires] Check, in order: * Prefer a long-running service (or scheduled) install; a one-off console session may not stay up for the hourly tick * Environment is not `preview`: auto-update is hard-disabled there * Activity-window guard is not holding it up: run `data-hub-watcher self-update`, or ask an admin to flag the release **mandatory** * **Last heartbeat** on the watcher’s page is recent; a stale watcher is not ticking Upgrade failure modes (`update_started` → `update_failed`, editable installs, missing Scheduled Task) are covered in [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher#manual-update-self-update) and [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases). ## Windows service [#windows-service] ### The service exits immediately [#the-service-exits-immediately] A config file that doesn't load (missing, unreadable, not saved as UTF-8, malformed, or with a value the watcher doesn't accept) stops the service. `watcher.log` has an error that starts with `Cannot load config`, followed by the reason. The error also gives the command that checks the file, in the form `data-hub-watcher --config "C:\path\to\config.yaml" config validate`. Run it as written, because without `--config` it checks the config file of whoever runs it, not the one the service uses. Fix what it reports and start the service again. An env file that isn't saved as UTF-8 stops the service the same way, with an error that starts with `Cannot load env file`. Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes UTF-16 for `>` and `>>`, so `echo X=Y >> .env.production` breaks a UTF-8 env file. Watchers before 1.4.2 wrote only a traceback to the Application event log for either problem. If it stops before writing to `watcher.log`: * Check `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\service-bootstrap.log` for a pre-dispatcher crash (missing `pywin32`, moved venv, corrupt install) * Query the Windows Application event log: ```powershell Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Where-Object { $_.ProviderName -match 'Python|DataHubWatcher' -or $_.Message -match 'DataHubWatcher' } | Format-List TimeCreated, ProviderName, Id, LevelDisplayName, Message ``` * Run the service in the foreground to see the traceback: ```powershell & "C:\path\to\venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m win32serviceutil debug DataHubWatcher ``` ### `self-update` says “Upgrade dispatched” but nothing happens [#self-update-says-upgrade-dispatched-but-nothing-happens] On Windows uv-tool installs, the upgrade runs out of process under SYSTEM and takes 30–60s. Track it: ```powershell Get-Service data-hub-watcher Get-Content ~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log -Tail 20 -Wait ``` ### Turn on debug logging for the service [#turn-on-debug-logging-for-the-service] Add `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` to the env file the service loads (typically `~/.data-hub/.env.`) and restart the service. No reinstall needed. This works with watcher 1.4.2 and later; earlier versions ignore the setting in the env file. ## Where are the logs? [#where-are-the-logs] Rotating logs (10 MB each, 5 backups). CLI `watch` and the Windows service share one file: | Platform | Log file | | ------------- | ------------------------------------------- | | Windows | `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\watcher.log` | | macOS / Linux | `~/.data-hub/watcher.log` | Add `--verbose` for debug console output: `data-hub-watcher --verbose watch`. Windows uv-tool upgrade output lands in `~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log`. ## API clients get `401 Unauthorized` [#api-clients-get-401-unauthorized] The bearer token is missing, mistyped, revoked, or expired. Check **Settings → Access Tokens** and re-issue if needed. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). A script that calls the watcher or processing routes with a browser session, instead of a token, also gets `401`. Those routes accept only personal access tokens; see [How a token acts](/docs/manage-tokens#how-a-token-acts). ## MCP clients get `401 Unauthorized` [#mcp-clients-get-401-unauthorized] MCP doesn’t accept personal access tokens, so a client configured with `Authorization: Bearer dhub_…` gets a 401 on every call. Remove the header, leave only the URL, and let the client run its sign-in flow. Setup per client is in [MCP overview](/docs/mcp#connect-a-client). An already-connected client that starts failing has usually lost its grant: sign in again from the client. If reads work and one tool fails with a missing-scope message, the client holds `read` but not `write`; reconnect and approve both. ## Ask an agent to diagnose it [#ask-an-agent-to-diagnose-it] Use the `troubleshoot_instrument` MCP prompt under [MCP prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts).

pages.markdown:
# Administration overview (/docs/administration)



**For:** Administrators

Admins keep the workspace healthy: confirm new instruments, watch the fleet, issue tokens, manage who is an admin, roll out watcher releases, and connect Linear and Slack. Admins can also delete any run comment and review the feedback people send about Data Hub.

The admin-only pages under **Settings** are **Feedback**, **Integrations**, **Watchers**, and **Members**. Members don’t see them in the settings menu. **Settings → Watchers** holds the release form and the list of every watcher; each instrument’s own watcher page is under the instrument, and members can read it.

Roles and scopes are defined in [Security and permissions](/docs/security). Day-to-day operator setup is in [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument).

pages.title: Manage instruments
pages.description: Review and confirm pending instruments, read an instrument’s status badge, watched folder, and file patterns, and edit its name and type.
pages.markdown: # Manage instruments (/docs/manage-instruments) **For:** Administrators When a lab operator registers an instrument from the watcher, it appears as `pending` and cannot upload until you confirm it. Operator-side setup is in [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). Retiring and reactivating are in [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument). ## Instrument states [#instrument-states] The **Instruments** page has tabs for active, pending, and retired instruments. | Status | UI label | Meaning | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | `pending` | Pending | Registered but not confirmed. Watchers cannot upload. | | `active` | Active | Confirmed and accepting uploads. | | `inactive` | Retired | Deactivated; no new uploads. Historical runs stay browsable. | Each instrument also has a status badge, which says whether its new files can arrive; see [Read an instrument’s page](#view-instrument-health). ## Confirm a pending instrument [#confirm-a-pending-instrument] Confirming opens a review of what the watcher was set up to do, so you can check it before files start to flow. Open the Data Hub web app and go to **Instruments**. Open the **Pending** tab (or find the amber **Pending** badge), and choose **Confirm…** on the instrument’s row. You can also open the pending instrument’s page, which has a **Waiting for confirmation** card with the same button. Read the review. It shows the instrument’s ID, which can’t be changed later, and what the watcher registered: the computer and the name of the token it registered with, the watch folder, the file patterns, how files become runs (a plain name for the preset, with one example from a recent or sample file name), and the upload mode. Choose an **Instrument type**. It’s required, because it decides how files are processed and which details appear on run pages. Choose **Confirm instrument**. The instrument becomes active and its type is saved in one step. If something in the review looks wrong, choose **Change settings first**. It opens the watcher’s **Settings** tab, which works for a pending instrument, so you can fix the folder or patterns before you confirm. See [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). After you confirm, the operator starts the watcher service on the PC (step 5 of [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument#start-the-watcher-service)), and the badge goes from **Connecting** to **Online** once the watcher checks in. If the watcher hasn’t checked in 15 minutes after you confirm, the badge turns **Offline** and its notice says the watcher never checked in. Members who open a pending instrument’s page see one line instead of the card: “This instrument is waiting for an admin to confirm it. Runs will appear here after that.” Confirming is admin-only for signed-in users. Under the hood it is `PATCH /api/v1/instruments/:id` with `status` and `instrument_type` together. Token automation uses the `instruments:write` scope instead. See the [generated API docs](/docs/api). ## Read an instrument’s page [#view-instrument-health] The top of each instrument page shows what you need to tell whether its files will reach Data Hub: * **Status badge**: **Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, **Offline**, **Pending**, or **Retired**, next to the instrument name. It follows the instrument’s one watcher, which checks in once a minute, so a watcher that was just restarted can take up to a minute to show as online. Hover over the badge for a short explanation, or select it to open the watcher’s page. Hostname and version are only on that page. The rules are in [Instrument status](/docs/concepts#instrument-status). * **Watched folder**: the folder the watcher reads from. Hover over it for a reminder that files saved anywhere else don’t appear, and select it to copy the path. * **File patterns**: the patterns the watcher uploads, such as `*.csv`. * **A note for manual upload mode**: “Files upload when someone requests them,” beside the patterns, whatever the badge says. When the badge reads **Offline**, a notice between the header and the runs table says why: the folder is missing, the watcher isn’t checking in, someone stopped it, or the instrument has no watcher. When the folder is missing, the watcher isn’t checking in, or someone stopped it, the notice offers **See details**, which opens the watcher’s **Activity** tab. For a missing folder, admins also get **Change folder**, which opens the watcher’s settings form with the **Watch folder** field selected. When the instrument has no watcher, or its watcher was deregistered, there is nothing current to look at: admins get **Connect a watcher**, which opens [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument), and members get no action. The notices are described from the scientist’s side in [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive). Files saved anywhere other than the watched folder, such as a shared network drive, don’t appear in Data Hub. Neither do files whose names don’t match a pattern. Admins can change the folder and patterns on the watcher’s **Settings** tab (watcher 1.4.0 and later); see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). You can also change them on the PC with `data-hub-watcher config edit`; see [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference). Watcher health comes from heartbeats; see [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers). ## Edit an instrument [#edit-an-instrument] The three-dot menu on an instrument page, and the row menu on the instruments table, hold the admin actions. Members see no menu on the instrument page, and reach the watcher page through the status badge. * **Edit details**: change the **Display name** and the **Instrument type** * **Watcher**: open the instrument’s watcher page, where its settings are * **Retire** or **Reactivate**: see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument) The instrument type decides which processor reads the instrument’s files, including DishCam and Aunty; see [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing). The instrument ID never changes, because it is the storage key prefix.

pages.title: Retire an instrument
pages.description: Retire an instrument so it stops accepting uploads and watchers, while keeping historical runs and files.
pages.markdown: # Retire an instrument (/docs/retire-an-instrument) **For:** Administrators Retire an instrument when it is decommissioned or out of service for a long stretch. Retirement sets status to `inactive` (shown as **Retired**), removes it from the sidebar and dashboard lists of live instruments, and stops new uploads. Nothing is deleted from storage; you can reactivate later. ## What retirement does [#what-retirement-does] When you retire an instrument: * Status becomes `inactive` (UI: **Retired**), with `retiredAt` / `retiredBy` audit fields * It stops accepting new runs and watchers * Its badge reads **Retired**, and its Upload buttons on run pages are turned off * All existing runs and files stay browsable * Its watcher is deregistered in the same request so it stops checking in. The watcher stays on the instrument’s watcher page as a past watcher Instrument IDs stay permanent. Retire rather than trying to rename or delete an instrument that has already produced data. ## Retire from the web app [#retire-from-the-web-app] Open the instrument’s page. Open the three-dot menu, which only admins see, and choose **Retire**. The row menu on **Instruments** has the same item. Confirm in the dialog. It lists how many runs are kept, says nothing is deleted from storage, and, when the instrument has a watcher, says its watcher will be deregistered so it stops checking in. The instrument moves to the **Retired** tab on **Instruments**. ## Reactivate [#reactivate] From a retired instrument’s page, open the three-dot menu and choose **Reactivate**. The row menu on the **Retired** tab has the same item. Status returns to `active` and the instrument reappears in the sidebar and dashboard. The watcher deregistered at retirement does **not** reconnect automatically. An operator must re-register it (usually `data-hub-watcher init` on the instrument PC) after reactivation. Until then the instrument’s badge reads **Offline**, with a notice that it isn’t connected to a watcher, and admins can follow **Connect a watcher** to [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). ## Via the API [#via-the-api] ```sh # Retire curl -X PATCH https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments/bio-rad-cfx96 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"status":"inactive"}' # Reactivate curl -X PATCH https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments/bio-rad-cfx96 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"status":"active"}' ``` Session callers need the admin role; bearer tokens need `instruments:write`.

pages.title: Issue and revoke tokens
pages.description: Create, use, and revoke personal access tokens that authenticate the watcher and other Data Hub API clients, and see what a token can and can’t do.
pages.markdown: # Issue and revoke tokens (/docs/manage-tokens) **For:** Administrators Personal access tokens authenticate the watcher, the processing Lambda, and scripts that call the Data Hub API. Creating and revoking tokens requires the workspace admin role. Members can view the list at **Settings → Access Tokens** but cannot create or delete tokens. Roles and scopes: [Security and permissions](/docs/security). ## How a token acts [#how-a-token-acts] A token acts as itself, under its own name. It doesn’t act as the admin who created it or as any other person. * Anything a token does is recorded under the token’s name: comments, deleting a run, retiring an instrument, removing a watcher, and notifications sent through the API. * Run pages, instrument pages, watcher pages, comments, and the notification bell show the token’s name with a key icon. * A token can post comments, and it can edit and delete only the comments it posted. Some actions need a signed-in person, so tokens can’t do them at all: claiming runs, sending feedback, and reviewing feedback. AI assistants aren’t affected, because they sign in as the person who approved them; see [MCP overview](/docs/mcp). The reverse also holds: the API routes that the watcher and the Lambda call accept only tokens. A browser session gets `401 Unauthorized` on watcher registration and heartbeats, upload links, file updates, run creation and updates, and instrument creation. ## Create a token [#create-a-token] ### In the web app [#in-the-web-app] Sign in as an admin. Go to **Settings → Access Tokens**. Click **Create token**. Enter a **Name** that identifies the client (for example, `FPLC watcher, Lab 201`). This is the name people see wherever the token acts, so make it recognizable. Pick an **Expiration**: 30 days, 90 days (the default), 1 year, or no expiry. Under **Scopes**, click a preset, or click **Customize scopes** to pick individual scopes. Click **Create token**. The plaintext token is shown once: copy it immediately. It starts with `dhub_` followed by a 64-character hex string. ### Scope presets [#scope-presets] A preset selects the minimum scopes a common client needs: * **Read-only**: view instruments, runs, files, watchers, and archive jobs; change nothing * **Watcher**: what a watcher needs to register, report runs, and upload files * **Lambda**: what the processing Lambda needs to read instruments and runs, and write run and file results The **Lambda** preset includes `runs:read`, which DishCam processing needs to pair each photo stack with its `run.json`. A Lambda token created from an older preset gets `403 FORBIDDEN` on DishCam files. Create a new token from the current preset and update the Lambda’s `DATA_HUB_API_KEY`; the [Lambda developer docs](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/lambda.md#supported-instrument-types) describe the swap. You cannot change a token’s scopes after creation. To change them, revoke the token and create a new one. ### Via the API [#via-the-api] Creating and deleting tokens is admin-only and needs a signed-in browser session (cookie). Tokens cannot manage other tokens. ```sh curl -X POST https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/tokens \ -H "Cookie: session_cookie_here" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "FPLC watcher", "scopes": ["instruments:read", "instruments:write", "watchers:read", "watchers:report", "runs:create", "runs:update", "runs:upload", "files:update"], "expires_at": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }' ``` `scopes` is required and must be a non-empty list of explicit scopes. The wildcard `*` and the older coarse scopes `runs:write`, `files:write`, and `watchers:write` are rejected. `expires_at` is optional; if omitted, the token never expires. The request is rejected if it includes `user_id`, because tokens don’t belong to a person. The response includes the plaintext once in the `token` field. ## Use a token [#use-a-token] ### With the watcher [#with-the-watcher] During `data-hub-watcher init`, paste the token when prompted. Or set it first: ```sh export DATA_HUB_API_KEY=dhub_your_token_here data-hub-watcher init ``` ### With the REST API [#with-the-rest-api] ```sh curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \ -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" ``` More in the [API overview](/docs/api). Tokens don’t authenticate MCP clients, which sign in with OAuth instead. See [MCP overview](/docs/mcp). ## View tokens [#view-tokens] **Settings → Access Tokens** lists every active token with these columns: * **Name** * **Created by**: the admin who made the token. For tokens created before October 6, 2026, this shows the person the token used to act as. * **Token**: the prefix only, because the full token is never stored * **Scopes** * **Last used** * **Expires** * **Created** ## Revoke a token [#revoke-a-token] Go to **Settings → Access Tokens**. Click the delete icon on the token’s row and confirm. The token stops working immediately. Clients using it start receiving `401 Unauthorized`. ```sh curl -X DELETE https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/tokens/ \ -H "Cookie: session_cookie_here" ``` A revoked token leaves the list, but Data Hub keeps its record. Wherever the token acted, its name stays visible and is marked **(revoked)**. ## After revoking a token [#after-revoking-a-token] If a running watcher used that token: Create a new token with the **Watcher** preset. On the instrument PC, re-run `data-hub-watcher init` and enter the new token. The new token takes over the existing watcher registration, so you don’t need to deregister the old one first. Restart the watcher (`data-hub-watcher watch` or the Windows service). ## When someone leaves [#when-someone-leaves] Tokens keep working after the admin who created them leaves or their account is deleted, because tokens act as themselves. When someone leaves, check the **Created by** column and revoke any of their tokens that nobody else should keep using. ## Token hygiene [#token-hygiene] * Name tokens so you can tell which PC or client each belongs to * Set expirations for temporary setups * Scope to least privilege; see [Token scopes](/docs/security#token-scopes) * Revoke immediately when a watcher is decommissioned or a token may have been exposed Tokens are hashed with SHA-256 before storage; plaintext is never persisted.

pages.title: Manage members
pages.description: Promote and demote workspace admins from Settings → Members.
pages.markdown: # Manage members (/docs/manage-members) **For:** Administrators Workspace members sign in with Google OAuth. Admins decide who else has the admin role. Member vs admin capabilities are summarized in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles). ## Open the members list [#open-the-members-list] Go to **Settings → Members**. Non-admins who open the URL see an “Admins only” message; the settings sidebar hides the entry for them. The table lists every signed-in user: name, email, role badge, and an **Admin** toggle. ## Promote or demote [#promote-or-demote] Toggle **Admin** on a row to grant or revoke admin access. Every privileged action re-checks the database, so the change applies to that user’s next one. Their view of the dashboard can lag by up to 5 minutes, because admin-only buttons and sidebar entries come from their [cached session](/docs/security#session-lifetime). You cannot demote yourself. That guard prevents locking the workspace out of its last admin. Ask another admin to demote you if needed. ## First admin bootstrap [#first-admin-bootstrap] The first admins come from the `ADMIN_EMAILS` environment variable (comma-separated, case-insensitive). Listed users are promoted on every sign-in. After that, any admin can promote others from this page. There is no invite flow in the product: people appear here after they sign in successfully to your deployment. Every Google account your OAuth client accepts can sign in, so that client, not this page, controls who appears here. See [Who can sign in](/docs/security#who-can-sign-in).

pages.title: Set up integrations
pages.description: Connect Data Hub to Linear for feedback reports, and to Slack for personal direct messages and a shared new-run channel, from Settings → Integrations.
pages.markdown: # Set up integrations (/docs/integrations) **For:** Administrators and engineers **Settings → Integrations** holds the connections the whole workspace shares. Only admins see it. The page has three parts: * **Linear**: where feedback reports go, and where their status comes from * **Slack app**: the credentials behind personal Slack direct messages and **Connect to Slack** * **Slack channel**: a webhook that posts a message to a shared channel whenever a new run arrives Each person’s own notification choices are separate, under **Settings → Notifications**. See [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications). ## How secrets are stored [#integration-secrets-key] Data Hub encrypts the secrets you paste on this page before saving them: the Linear client secret and signing secret, and the Slack bot token and client secret. It never shows a saved secret again. To change one, paste a new value and save. Encryption needs the `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` environment variable on the web app. It is 64 hexadecimal characters; generate one with `openssl rand -hex 32`, set it in Vercel, and redeploy. Until it is set, saving a secret fails, and the Slack app card says so. If the key changes after secrets were saved, Data Hub can’t read them anymore. The affected field says **Can’t read saved value**. Put the old key back, or paste the value again and save. ## Linear for feedback reports [#linear] Feedback that people send from Data Hub becomes an issue in your Linear workspace, and the report’s status follows that issue. Until an admin saves a Linear team here, the **Feedback** item stays out of the account menu, and sending feedback through the API or an AI assistant returns an error saying feedback isn’t set up. What reporters see is in [Send feedback](/docs/send-feedback). The Linear card walks you through four steps. ### 1. Connect your Linear app [#linear-connect] Data Hub signs in to Linear as an app, so you create one app in Linear for it. In Linear, go to **Settings → API → OAuth applications** and create a new application. Name it **Data Hub**. Linear shows this name on every issue it files. Linear asks for a callback URL. Data Hub doesn’t use one, so paste the URL shown in the step, which is your deployment’s address. Turn on **Client credentials**, then save. Copy the client ID and client secret into the Linear card in Data Hub, and choose **Connect**. Data Hub checks the credentials with Linear before it saves them. If client credentials are turned off for the app, the card says so; turn them on in the app’s settings in Linear and choose **Connect** again. If the credentials belong to a different Linear workspace than the one already connected, Data Hub asks before switching. Switching clears the team, project, labels, and signing secret. Issues already in Linear stay there. ### 2. Choose where reports go [#linear-destination] Pick the **Team** that receives reports. Only public teams are listed, because Linear doesn’t show private teams to apps. Optionally pick a **Project**. Optionally pick a label for each kind of report: **Bug**, **Feature request**, and **Other**. Labels can come from the team or from the whole workspace. Linear adds the matching label to each new issue. Choose **Save and turn on feedback**. Everyone sees **Feedback** in their account menu from then on. Changing the team later clears the project and labels. Status updates also stop until the Linear webhook from step 3 points at the new team. ### 3. Get status updates from Linear [#linear-status-updates] A webhook tells Data Hub when an issue changes, so it can update the report and tell the person who sent it when the issue closes. In Linear, go to **Settings → API** and choose **New webhook**. Paste the **Webhook URL** shown in the step. It ends in `/api/v1/integrations/linear/webhook`. For **Team**, choose the team from step 2. Under events, turn on **Issues** only. Save the webhook, then copy its signing secret into **Signing secret** in Data Hub and save. Data Hub uses the signing secret to check that each update really comes from Linear. The step shows **Waiting for an update from Linear** until the first one arrives. Any change to an issue in the team sends one, including the test report in the next step. ### 4. Send a test report [#linear-test-report] Choose **Send test report**. Data Hub files a report as you and links to the new Linear issue. Move that issue to **Done** in Linear. The step confirms that the issue closed and that you got a Data Hub notification. You can also skip the test. ### After setup [#linear-after-setup] Once setup is finished, the Linear card shows a summary: the connected workspace, where reports go, whether status updates are working and when the last one arrived, and what reporters see for each Linear status. | When the Linear issue moves to | The reporter sees | | --------------------------------------- | ----------------- | | **Done**, or any other completed status | Resolved | | **Canceled** | Declined | | **Duplicate** | Declined | | Any other status | Open | Data Hub notifies the reporter once, when the issue first closes. Moving an issue from one closed status to another, such as **Done** to **Released**, doesn’t notify again. Reopening an issue and closing it again does. If Data Hub keeps rejecting updates from Linear, **Status updates** shows **Not working**. The usual cause is a wrong signing secret, or Linear turning the webhook off after repeated failures. Paste the signing secret again from the webhook’s page in Linear, and check that the webhook is still turned on. **Disconnect Linear** turns feedback off. Issues already in Linear stay there. ## Slack app for direct messages [#slack-app] Personal Slack direct messages and the **Connect to Slack** button use one shared Slack app. Create the app once in the [Slack API portal](https://api.slack.com/apps), then give Data Hub its credentials. You can reuse an existing Slack app, including the one behind the channel webhook. ### Create the app [#create-the-slack-app] In the Slack API portal, choose **Create New App → From scratch**, or open an existing app. Under **OAuth & Permissions**, add these scopes: **Bot Token Scopes:** | Scope | Purpose | | ------------ | -------------------------------------------- | | `chat:write` | Send direct messages with `chat.postMessage` | **User Token Scopes:** | Scope | Purpose | | --------- | ----------------------------------- | | `openid` | Sign in with Slack (OpenID Connect) | | `profile` | Display name in the identity token | Under **Redirect URLs**, add one callback URL per environment. The path is always `/api/v1/settings/slack/callback`: | Environment | Example URL | | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Local | `http://localhost:3000/api/v1/settings/slack/callback` | | Staging | `https://staging.datahub.example.com/api/v1/settings/slack/callback` | | Production | `https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/settings/slack/callback` | `SLACK_REDIRECT_URI`, or the request origin plus that path when unset, must match a listed URL exactly. Under **Install App**, choose **Install to Workspace** (or **Reinstall** after changing scopes). ### Give Data Hub the credentials [#slack-app-credentials] Enter the credentials in the **Slack app** card under **Settings → Integrations**, or set them as environment variables on the web app. A value saved in the card takes effect right away, with no redeploy, and is used instead of the matching environment variable. | Card field | Environment variable | Where to find it | Required | | ------------------------ | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | **Bot token** | `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` | **Install App** → Bot User OAuth Token (`xoxb-…`) | Yes | | **Client ID** | `SLACK_CLIENT_ID` | **Basic Information** → App Credentials | Yes | | **Client secret** | `SLACK_CLIENT_SECRET` | **Basic Information** → App Credentials | Yes | | **Allowed workspace ID** | `SLACK_TEAM_ID` | Workspace URL segment `T…` in `app.slack.com/client/T…` | No, but recommended so connections stay on your workspace | Each field shows where its value comes from: **Saved here**, **Using** followed by the variable name, or **Not set**. **Remove saved value** makes the environment variable the source again. If Data Hub can’t read a saved value, for example because `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` changed, it uses the environment variable in the meantime. Two settings exist only as environment variables, and changing them needs a redeploy: | Variable | Purpose | Required | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- | | `SLACK_STATE_SECRET` | Signs the short-lived value Data Hub checks while a person connects Slack. Generate with `openssl rand -base64 32` | No (falls back to `AUTH_SECRET`) | | `SLACK_REDIRECT_URI` | Full callback URL, when it differs from the request origin | No | Members can then connect under **Settings → Notifications**. Deploy runbooks are linked from [Deploy Data Hub](/docs/self-hosting). ## Slack channel for new runs [#slack-channel] The **Slack channel** card holds a Slack incoming webhook. Data Hub posts one message to that channel each time a new run is reported. This is separate from personal direct messages, which each person turns on for themselves. In your Slack app, open **Incoming Webhooks**, turn them on, and add a webhook for the channel you want. Copy the webhook URL. It starts with `https://hooks.slack.com/services/`. Paste it into the **Slack channel** card and save. The card shows **Configured** and who last changed it. To change channels, paste a new webhook URL. To stop the messages, remove the webhook. This setting has no environment variable.

pages.markdown:
# Overview (/docs/api)



**For:** Developers and integrators

The Data Hub API is served by the web application at `/api/v1/`. The watcher, Lambda, and dashboard all call it. Data Hub is self-hosted, so the base URL is your deployment host plus `/api/v1`. Examples use `https://datahub.example.com`; substitute your host.

Per-endpoint request and response shapes live in the generated pages under this section (same sidebar). Each deployment also publishes OpenAPI 3.1 at `/api/v1/openapi.json`.

## Authentication [#authentication]

Two methods (full model in [Security and permissions](/docs/security)):

* **Session cookies**: web dashboard (Google OAuth). Session callers implicitly hold every scope.
* **Bearer tokens**: `Authorization: Bearer dhub_…` for the watcher, the Lambda, and scripts

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here"
```

Every token request needs a [scope](/docs/security#token-scopes). A missing scope returns `403 FORBIDDEN`. Some mutations also require the admin role; see [Admin-gated operations](/docs/security#admin-gated-operations).

Some routes accept only one of the two methods:

* The routes the watcher and the Lambda call accept only tokens, and return `401 UNAUTHORIZED` to a session. These cover watcher registration and heartbeats, upload links, file updates, run creation and updates, and instrument creation.
* Claiming runs, sending feedback, reviewing feedback, and managing tokens need a signed-in person, so tokens can’t call them.

Mint tokens in the UI: [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

## First request [#first-request]

List instruments:

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here"
```

Fetch the OpenAPI document (no auth required):

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/openapi.json
```

The document covers the integrator surface: instruments, runs, comments, lab notebook links, files, watchers, archive jobs, search, and `POST /notifications/dispatch`. Routes that only the dashboard uses are left out: `/tokens`, `/users`, `/feedback`, `/settings/*`, and the notification inbox. The MCP transport is documented separately.

## Instruments and their watcher [#instrument-connection]

An instrument has at most one active watcher, so `GET /instruments` and `GET /instruments/:id` describe it with one object, not counts:

* `watcher`: the instrument’s active watcher, or `null` when it has none. It carries `id`, `status`, `status_reason`, `last_heartbeat_at`, `file_patterns`, `upload_mode`, and `config_state`. With the `watchers:read` scope it also carries the fields that say where the watcher runs: `hostname`, `os_info`, `version`, `watch_directory`, and `shared_computer_with`. A token that has `instruments:read` but not `watchers:read` gets the watcher without those five fields; they are missing from the object, not `null`. A signed-in browser session has every scope, so it always gets them.
* `connection`: whether new files can reach Data Hub. `state` is `online`, `restarting`, `connecting`, or `offline`, and `reason` says why it is offline (`folder_missing`, `unresponsive`, `never_checked_in`, `stopped`, `no_watcher`, or `deregistered`) and is `null` otherwise. The rules are the ones behind the badge in the web app; see [Instrument status](/docs/concepts#instrument-status). `connection` ignores the instrument’s own `status`, so a `pending` instrument can be `online`. The web app shows **Pending** or **Retired** first, and `connection.state` only after that.
* `past_watcher_count`: how many deregistered watchers the instrument has had.

`GET /instruments/:id` still returns `watcher_count`, but it is deprecated. It keeps its old value for now. A later release will remove it, and the changelog will announce the date first. Read `watcher` instead, which is `null` when there is none.

`GET /search` returns the same instrument results as the `global_search` MCP tool. An instrument result now carries `connection`, and its `watcherStatus` and `lastWatcherHeartbeatAt` are deprecated. They keep their old values for now, and `connection` replaces them.

## Actions taken by a token [#actions-taken-by-a-token]

A token acts under its own name, not as a person, so responses name the token when it did something:

* A comment posted by a token has `user: null` and a `token` object with the token’s `id` and `name`. A comment posted by a person has `token: null`.
* A run deleted by a token has `deleted_by_token` set, alongside `deleted_at`.
* A lab notebook link added or last edited by a token has `created_by_token` or `updated_by_token` set, and `created_by` or `updated_by` null.

Read both fields when you display who did something. See [How a token acts](/docs/manage-tokens#how-a-token-acts).

## Send notifications [#send-notifications]

`POST /notifications/dispatch` sends a short message to chosen people, with an optional link to a run. It needs a token with the `notifications:create` scope. Each person’s **Service notifications** setting decides whether the message appears in the notification bell, as a Slack direct message, or both. The message shows the token’s name as its sender. Request fields are on the generated [dispatch notifications](/docs/api/notifications/dispatchNotifications) page.

## Pagination and filtering [#pagination-and-filtering]

List endpoints that return pages (notably run search) accept:

* `page`: 1-based page index
* `per_page`: page size, 1 to 100

Responses include pagination metadata such as `page`, `per_page`, `total`, and `total_pages`.

Run report items page by index instead, with `offset` and `limit` (max 200). Their responses return `offset`, `limit`, and `total`.

Run search also supports filters (instrument, date range, attribution via `ranBy`, and instrument-specific metadata). Exact query parameters are on each generated operation page in the sidebar under this **API** section.

## Error responses [#error-responses]

Errors use a nested envelope:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Instrument not found.",
    "details": null
  }
}
```

Common codes: `VALIDATION_ERROR` (400), `UNAUTHORIZED` (401), `FORBIDDEN` (403), `NOT_FOUND` (404), `CONFLICT` (409). Scope failures use `code: "FORBIDDEN"` with a message naming the missing scope.

Feedback routes have two more. `LINEAR_UNAVAILABLE` (502) means Data Hub couldn’t reach Linear, where reports are stored. `FEEDBACK_NOT_CONFIGURED` (503) means no admin has connected Linear yet; see [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations#linear).

## MCP [#mcp]

`GET` and `POST` `/mcp/v1` expose the MCP server over Streamable HTTP, outside the `/api/v1` tree. Clients authenticate with OAuth rather than a personal access token, and hold `read` to connect plus `write` to call any tool that changes data. See [MCP overview](/docs/mcp).

pages.title: Overview
pages.description: Connect an AI client to Data Hub over the Model Context Protocol, including OAuth sign-in, the read and write scopes, and per-client setup.
pages.markdown: # Overview (/docs/mcp) **For:** Developers and integrators Data Hub exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `/mcp/v1` so AI clients can query instruments, runs, files, and watcher health. Clients authenticate by sending you through a browser sign-in. Catalogs for [tools](/docs/mcp/tools), [prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts), and [resources](/docs/mcp/resources) are generated from the live server schema, so they match what your client discovers when it connects. ## Authentication [#authentication] The MCP server authenticates with OAuth. All you need to provide is the endpoint URL; for example, `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1`. The first connection opens your browser: Sign in to Data Hub with Google, unless you already have a session open. Read the **Authorize application** screen. It names the client, the host it redirects to, and the access it’s asking for. Click **Allow**. Your client stores the access token it receives and renews it without asking again. **Allow** grants everything on the screen: there are no per-permission checkboxes, so click **Deny** if any line looks wrong. ### Scopes [#scopes] MCP uses two scopes rather than the `:` scopes that gate REST requests: * **`read`**: required to connect at all, and covers every read-only tool, resource, and prompt * **`write`**: additionally required by tools that change something, including claiming runs, commenting, adding lab notebook links, requesting uploads, reprocessing, and deleting Most clients ask for both, because the server advertises both. A client granted only `read` still connects and still reads; its first mutating tool call fails with a message naming the missing scope. Each entry in the [tools catalog](/docs/mcp/tools) lists the scope its REST equivalent requires, which tells you what data the tool touches. Over MCP, only `read` and `write` are enforced. The client acts as you, with your role. Admin-only actions, such as deleting someone else’s comment, work over MCP only when you are an admin. Claiming runs and sending feedback work because a signed-in person is behind the client, even though API tokens can’t do either. ## Connect a client [#connect-a-client] Examples use `https://datahub.example.com`; substitute your deployment host. ### Claude Code [#claude-code] Register the server with [`claude mcp add`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart). Run this in your terminal, not inside a `claude` session: ```bash claude mcp add --transport http --scope user data-hub https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1 ``` Confirm that the server was added by running `claude mcp list`. Then, start a session with `claude` and run `/mcp` to authenticate. ### Claude Desktop [#claude-desktop] Remote servers go through **Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector**. The `claude_desktop_config.json` file handles local servers only. Paste `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1` as the URL, click **Add**, then click **Connect** to sign in. Leave the OAuth client fields under **Advanced settings** empty, since Data Hub registers clients on demand. Claude reaches your server from Anthropic’s infrastructure rather than from your own machine, so the deployment has to be reachable from the public internet. A deployment running on `localhost` can’t be added this way; use Claude Code or Cursor for local work. ### Cursor [#cursor] Add the server to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project: ```json { "mcpServers": { "data-hub": { "url": "https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1" } } } ``` Open **Settings → Tools & MCP**. The server appears with a **Needs authentication** label; click it to start the browser flow. The tools show up once you approve the grant. ### Other clients [#other-clients] Any client that speaks Streamable HTTP and the MCP authorization spec needs one setting, the URL `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1`. For local development, point at `http://localhost:3000/mcp/v1` instead. Clients that speak MCP but not OAuth can bridge through [`mcp-remote`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-remote), which runs the browser flow on their behalf. ## Instruments and their watcher [#instrument-connection] `list_instruments` and `get_instrument` describe an instrument’s one active watcher with a `watcher` object, which is `null` when it has none, and say whether new files can reach Data Hub with `connection`, whose `state` is `online`, `restarting`, `connecting`, or `offline`, with a `reason` when it is offline. Both also return `pastWatcherCount`. The fields match the REST API’s, in camelCase; see [Instruments and their watcher](/docs/api#instrument-connection). MCP signs you in with OAuth, not a token with chosen scopes, so `watcher` always includes where the watcher runs, as `list_watchers` and `get_watcher` do. These older fields still come back with the values they had, but are deprecated, and the [tools catalog](/docs/mcp/tools) marks each one with the field to use instead: * `watcherCount`, `watchersOnline`, `lastWatcherHeartbeatAt`, and `activeWatcherId`, from both tools * `watchersOffline`, `activeWatcherHostname`, `activeWatcherWatchDirectory`, and `activeWatcherDeregistered`, from `get_instrument` only * `hasDeregisteredWatcher`, from `list_instruments` only * the top-level `filePatterns`, from both tools, which `watcher.filePatterns` replaces * `watcherStatus` and `lastWatcherHeartbeatAt` on an instrument result of `global_search`, which `connection` replaces * `watcherStatus` on each instrument of `get_system_status`, which now returns `connection` as well and which `connection` replaces ## Questions about Data Hub [#questions-about-data-hub] The assistant can answer questions about Data Hub itself, such as how to install a watcher, what a run status means, or what changed last week. It searches the documentation or the [changelog](/docs/send-feedback#changelog), reads what fits, and links it in its answer. Three tools do this, and all need only the `read` scope: * `search_docs` returns up to five matching sections of the docs, each with a short excerpt and a link * `read_doc` returns one docs page, or one section of a page, as Markdown * `search_changelog` lists changelog entries by date, or finds them by topic, and returns each one in full with a link that opens it in the Changelog Ask it what changed this week, what’s new since a date, or when something changed. Dates are calendar days, and both ends count. The answers come from the docs and changelog that ship with your deployment, so they match the version you run, including a staging deployment that is ahead of the published site. A change appears in the changelog once it has reached your deployment. Clients that let you attach resources by hand can also attach any docs page as `datahub://docs/`, for example `datahub://docs/manage-tokens`. The assistant reads the guides and the changelog. It doesn’t read the generated [API](/docs/api) endpoint pages or the [tools](/docs/mcp/tools), [prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts), and [resources](/docs/mcp/resources) catalogs, because the client already receives the catalog when it connects. When the docs don’t cover a question, the assistant says so and offers to [send feedback](#feedback) about the gap. ## Interactive run reports [#interactive-run-reports] Clients that support MCP Apps, an extension of the Model Context Protocol, show the same interactive run report as the web app when the assistant calls `get_run_report`. The report includes image carousels, plate maps, and the Aunty plate with its well charts. Clients without MCP Apps support get the same data as text and describe it instead. ## Feedback [#feedback] The assistant can send [feedback about Data Hub](/docs/send-feedback) for you, for example after a tool call fails. It shows you the draft first and sends it only after you agree. Sending feedback needs only the `read` scope. The assistant can also list the reports you sent and read one in full, by report ID or by Linear issue ID such as `ENG-1476`. Feedback tools return an error saying feedback isn’t set up until an admin [connects Linear](/docs/integrations#linear). Problems with one run’s data belong in a run comment instead, which the assistant can also post. ## Machine-readable catalog [#machine-readable-catalog] Fetch the same catalog these pages render from: ```bash curl https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1/schema.json ``` It lists every tool, prompt, and resource, with JSON Schema for arguments and each tool's response. The schema document needs no authentication.

pages.description: Short definitions of the Data Hub vocabulary: instruments, watchers, runs, statuses, processing, and access.
pages.markdown:
# Concepts (/docs/concepts)



**For:** Everyone

Short definitions of the vocabulary the rest of these docs use. If you’ve arrived mid-page and a term is unfamiliar, it’s defined here. Terms are grouped by what they describe: the equipment, the data, the rules that turn files into runs, and who can do what.

## Equipment and fleet [#equipment-and-fleet]

### Instrument [#instrument]

A piece of lab equipment registered in Data Hub, identified by a kebab-case **instrument ID** (e.g., `akta-fplc`, `plate-sealer-a`). The ID is permanent, because it becomes the storage key prefix and the identifier used across the system. A human-readable display name sits alongside it.

An instrument has three states. The **Instruments** page groups them into a tab per state, and a status badge beside each name shows whether new files can reach Data Hub:

| State      | Shown as                                                                                 | Meaning                                                                      |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pending`  | **Pending** tab, with a **Pending** badge                                                | Registered but not yet confirmed by an admin. A watcher can’t upload for it. |
| `active`   | **Active** tab, with an **Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, or **Offline** badge | Confirmed and accepting uploads.                                             |
| `inactive` | **Retired** tab, with a **Retired** badge                                                | Deactivated. No longer accepting uploads, but its runs stay browsable.       |

See [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument), [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments), and [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument).

### Instrument type [#instrument-type]

Separate from the instrument ID. The type tells Data Hub which [preprocessor](#preprocessor) to run on files from this instrument, so it controls what metadata, badges, and reports you get.

Admins set it from the instrument page: open the three-dot menu, choose **Edit details**, and pick a supported type. An instrument with no matching type still stores and serves raw files. It gets no extracted metadata and no processed artifacts. See [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing).

### Instrument status [#instrument-status]

The badge beside an instrument’s name, in the instruments table, on Home, and in search results. It answers one question: will new files from this instrument show up? It is built for the people who use the instrument, so it doesn’t show the watcher’s detail. On an instrument’s page and in the instruments table, select the badge to open the instrument’s [watcher page](/docs/manage-watchers#the-watcher-page). In search results the whole row is the link, so the badge there is a label only. Hover over it, or focus it with the keyboard, for a one-sentence explanation.

| Badge          | When it shows                                                                                                                                                                   | What it means                                                                                             |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Pending**    | The instrument isn’t confirmed yet. This wins over everything below, even when its watcher is checking in.                                                                      | Waiting for an admin to confirm this instrument.                                                          |
| **Retired**    | The instrument is retired. This wins over the watcher’s state.                                                                                                                  | This instrument no longer takes new runs. Its runs stay browsable.                                        |
| **Connecting** | The watcher registered but hasn’t sent its first heartbeat, and 15 minutes haven’t passed since it registered or since an admin confirmed the instrument, whichever came later. | The watcher was just set up and hasn’t checked in yet.                                                    |
| **Restarting** | The watcher stopped for a Windows restart or an automatic update less than 15 minutes ago.                                                                                      | The instrument PC is restarting or updating. This usually takes a minute or two.                          |
| **Online**     | The watcher is watching and its last heartbeat is less than 5 minutes old.                                                                                                      | New files upload automatically, or when someone requests them if the instrument is in manual upload mode. |
| **Offline**    | Anything else: the instrument has no watcher, or its watcher was deregistered; the watcher is silent, never checked in, stopped by someone, or can’t find its watch folder.     | New files won’t appear right now. A notice on the instrument page says why.                               |

Only the watcher’s own state decides **Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, and **Offline**. A pending change to the watcher’s settings never changes the badge. An instrument that is **Offline** shows a notice with the reason; see [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive). If it stays **Offline** for 30 minutes, people who subscribe to it are notified; see [When an instrument goes offline](/docs/configure-notifications#instrument-offline).

### Watcher [#watcher]

The `data-hub-watcher` command-line program that runs on an instrument PC. It monitors a directory, groups new files into runs, uploads them to cloud storage, and reports status to the API. Each instrument can have at most one active watcher at a time.

A watcher is registered with the API and carries one registration ID per [environment](#environment). Each instrument’s watcher has its own page, under the instrument, with its activity, health, and settings. Deregistering a watcher is a [soft delete](#soft-delete): the instrument keeps it as a past watcher, and its history stays visible for auditing. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers).

### Watcher status [#watcher-status]

What a watcher’s page, and **Settings → Watchers** for admins, show for each watcher, derived from its most recent [heartbeat](#heartbeat):

| Status                        | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Online**                    | A heartbeat arrived in the last 5 minutes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Unresponsive**              | No heartbeat for more than 5 minutes. The process crashed, the PC is off, or the network is blocking the API. A watcher that stopped for a Windows restart or shutdown, or for an automatic update, shows **Unresponsive** after 15 minutes instead. So does a watcher that never sent its first heartbeat, 15 minutes after it registered or its instrument was confirmed; hovering over its badge says it never checked in. |
| **Stopped**                   | The watcher shut down cleanly and said so in its last heartbeat. After a stop you chose, such as `data-hub-watcher service stop`, it keeps showing **Stopped**, however long ago that was, until it starts again. After a Windows restart or shutdown, or the stop of an automatic update, it shows **Stopped** for 15 minutes, then **Unresponsive** if it hasn’t returned.                                                  |
| **Waiting: folder not found** | The watcher is running and sending heartbeats, but its watch folder is missing, so it isn’t watching anything. A watcher goes into this state when it starts without the folder (watcher 1.4.0 and later), and when the folder disappears while it runs (watcher 1.4.3 and later). It starts watching again once the folder is back.                                                                                          |
| **Registered**                | The watcher registered but hasn’t sent its first heartbeat yet. It shows **Unresponsive** once 15 minutes pass after it registered, or after an admin confirmed its instrument if that came later. While the instrument is pending it stays **Registered**, because the watcher won’t start until the instrument is confirmed.                                                                                                |
| **Deregistered**              | A past watcher. Someone deregistered it, or retired its instrument. Its page is read-only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

A watcher that stopped because Windows is restarting or shutting down (watcher 1.4.1 and later), or because it is installing an automatic update (watcher 1.4.2 and later), is expected back. It shows **Stopped**, and hovering over the badge tells you when it starts showing **Unresponsive** if it hasn’t returned: 15 minutes after its last heartbeat. Any other stop, such as `data-hub-watcher service stop` or Ctrl+C, shows **Stopped** until the watcher starts again.

An unresponsive watcher keeps its registration and history, so you can read its last events to work out what happened. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher).

Instruments show a simpler summary of this status, the [instrument status](#instrument-status) badge. An instrument has one active watcher, so the badge follows that watcher; an instrument with no active watcher reads **Offline**.

### Heartbeat [#heartbeat]

A status ping the watcher sends to the API every 60 seconds. It carries the watcher version, instrument ID, watch directory, upload mode, activity counters, and uptime, and it drives **Last heartbeat** on the watcher’s page, the status badges, and the connectivity grid on the **Health** tab. The same tick runs the auto-updater. The upload queue is checked separately, also once a minute, so a slow upload can’t delay a heartbeat. With watcher 1.4.3 and later, the counts of a heartbeat that fails to send go out with the next one, so an outage doesn’t lose them. Older watchers lose them.

### Events [#events]

A per-watcher log of lifecycle moments and errors: `watcher_started`, `run_reported`, `file_uploaded`, `update_succeeded`, and `error` (with a `details.kind` discriminator), among others. Events are batched and flushed on each heartbeat and are shown on the watcher’s **Activity** tab, with a plain label and message for each, which makes them the primary tool for diagnosing a watcher remotely. With watcher 1.4.3 and later, the watcher keeps the events it hasn’t sent in its state file on the PC. An event that Data Hub couldn’t take at the time is sent with a later heartbeat while the watcher runs, and one that was queued when the watcher was stopped or killed is sent after the next start. Either way it keeps its original time. An event that Data Hub refuses as invalid isn’t sent again, and nor is one that Data Hub answers with a server error three heartbeats in a row; an `events_dropped` event records how many were lost. Older watchers lose those events. Data Hub writes some events itself, such as `upload_requests_cancelled`, which it records when someone deletes a run that has requested uploads. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher).

### Environment [#environment]

Which Data Hub deployment a watcher talks to: `staging`, `production`, or `preview` (a Vercel preview deployment, which needs an explicit API base URL). Staging and production are separate deployments with separate databases, so a single PC keeps an independent registration and local state per environment and can switch between them.

## Data [#data]

### Run [#run]

A logical grouping of files produced by one acquisition. The watcher assigns each file a **run ID** using its configured [run detection](#run-detection) method, then reports the run to the API. The first file for a run creates it; later files are added incrementally to the same run’s manifest. Spaces at the start or end of a run ID are ignored, so a run ID of `RUN001` with a space after it is the same run as `RUN001`.

### Run status [#run-status]

How far a run’s files have got from the instrument to the dashboard. These are the values you can filter by under **Add filter** on any run list:

| Status            | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Failed            | At least one file stopped on an error. [Reprocess](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-and-delete) after a fix.                                                                                              |
| Stalled           | At least one file has been processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing. Reprocess it to try again.                                                                                         |
| Upload failed     | The watcher gave up on at least one file, for example because its folder is no longer on the instrument PC. The file’s status says why. See [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). |
| Waiting to upload | Files are on their way from the instrument PC: someone requested them, or the watcher uploads them on its own.                                                                                       |
| Uploaded          | The files are in storage. Processing hasn’t started, or this instrument type has no preprocessor.                                                                                                    |
| Queued            | You chose **Reprocess**, and the files are waiting for a free processing slot. They start as other files finish. See [How reprocessing is queued](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-queue).                |
| Processing        | The preprocessor is reading the files, extracting metadata, and building reports.                                                                                                                    |
| Not uploaded      | Some files are only on the instrument PC, and nothing will upload them until someone requests them.                                                                                                  |
| Completed         | Processing finished.                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Empty             | The run has no files.                                                                                                                                                                                |

When a run’s files are in different states, the run shows the first status in this table that applies. The filter value `pending`, from before **Pending upload** was split, still matches **Waiting to upload** and **Not uploaded**.

### File and file category [#file-and-file-category]

Every file in a run carries a category, shown as a label in the run’s files table:

* **Raw**: what the instrument wrote, uploaded unchanged
* **Processed**: what a [preprocessor](#preprocessor) generated from a raw file, such as a CSV of well values, a contrast-adjusted PNG, or a preview JPG

Both categories download the same way, and file filters on the run page work on this label. See [Download files](/docs/browse-runs#download-files).

### Preprocessor [#preprocessor]

The server-side code that reads a raw file, extracts metadata, and writes processed files. It runs in an AWS Lambda when a file arrives in raw storage, or when you choose **Reprocess**. Reprocessing starts at most 10 files at a time and queues the rest; see [How reprocessing is queued](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-queue). Which preprocessor runs depends on the [instrument type](#instrument-type), and not every type has one. Per-type inputs and outputs are in [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing).

### Run archive [#run-archive]

The zip that **Download all** builds for a run. It covers the run’s active files and respects any file filter you have applied. Large archives build in the background as an archive job, so the first request can return a wait time rather than a file.

### Attribution [#attribution]

The record of who ran a run. Use **Claim** on the run to attribute yourself. Attribution is self-only: you claim or unclaim your own user, and you can’t attribute someone else. API tokens can’t claim runs. Claims drive **My runs** and the “ran by” filters, and claiming a run subscribes you to its comments. See [Claim who ran it](/docs/browse-runs#claim-who-ran-it).

### Lab notebook link [#lab-notebook-link]

A link from a run to a lab notebook page for its experiment, on any site, with an optional label. A run can have several. Anyone signed in can add, edit, or remove them, and global search finds runs by a pasted notebook URL. See [Link a run to its lab notebook](/docs/browse-runs#lab-notebook).

## Turning files into runs [#turning-files-into-runs]

### Run detection [#run-detection]

The rule that maps a file to a run ID. Two broad strategies:

* **Prefix**: a regex extracts the run ID from the filename. The default `^([^_]+)` takes everything before the first underscore, so `RUN001_data.csv` → `RUN001`
* **Directory**: each subdirectory under the watch directory is its own run, so `RUN001/data.csv` → `RUN001`

The full set of presets, and the custom-regex option, is in the [Configuration reference](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection).

### Stability period [#stability-period]

How many seconds a file must stay unchanged (same size and modification time) before the watcher treats it as fully written and eligible for upload. The default is 5 seconds; raise it for instruments that write large files slowly. A file that keeps changing past `max_stability_wait_seconds` (default 300, or 5 minutes) is abandoned with a `stability_timeout` error event. A file that the instrument keeps open after its last write can look finished while the watcher still can’t read it. Watcher 1.4.2 and later try it again every minute and upload it once the instrument lets go of it. Older watchers try it again only the next time they start.

### Upload mode [#upload-mode]

How files get from the instrument to cloud storage:

* **auto**: files upload immediately after they’re detected and stabilized. With watcher 1.2.1 and later, the watcher also uploads files someone requests from the run page
* **manual**: runs are reported to the server, but files aren’t uploaded until approved through the server-side upload queue, which the watcher checks once a minute. Use this when uploads need human approval

### Initial scan [#initial-scan]

What the watcher does with files already sitting in the watch directory the first time an environment is entered. `production` uploads the existing backlog (`full`). `staging` and `preview` record it as a baseline and skip it (`new-only`), so test environments aren’t flooded with history. See the [Configuration reference](/docs/configuration-reference#initial-scan).

### Dismiss [#dismiss]

For instruments in [manual upload mode](#upload-mode), dismissing a detected file, or one whose upload failed, tells the watcher not to upload it. Dismissing differs from deleting: the file never reached Data Hub storage, so there’s nothing to restore. A dismissed file stays dismissed, even if the watcher reports it again. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads).

The watcher reports a path only once, so a different file that the instrument later writes at the same path doesn’t appear on its own. It appears when the watcher reports that path again, which happens after `data-hub-watcher state forget`, or when the watcher starts without its saved record of what it has reported, for example after a reinstall. Data Hub then detects the file as new when its size or creation time differs from the dismissed file’s. On Linux, the modification time stands in for the creation time. The dismissed file stays dismissed.

Because Data Hub compares only size and time, two cases can surprise you:

* A new file the same size as the dismissed one counts as the same file when it keeps the old creation time, so it stays dismissed. On Windows and macOS this happens when the instrument overwrites the file in place. On Windows it can also happen when the file is deleted and written again, or saved through a temporary copy, within about 15 seconds.
* Copying a folder, for example with Explorer or `xcopy` on Windows or `cp` without `-p` on Linux, gives the copies new times. After you replace an instrument PC or restore its folder from a backup, a new watcher that scans the copied folder reports the files you dismissed as new detected files. Dismiss them again.

### Soft delete [#soft-delete]

Data Hub marks things deleted rather than erasing them, so history survives for auditing. Deleting a run hides it from run lists without removing its stored files, and **Show deleted runs** brings it back into view. It also cancels any uploads that were requested for the run’s files, and restoring the run doesn’t bring them back. Deregistering a watcher keeps its events and heartbeats. Anyone signed in can restore a deleted run from the run page.

## People and access [#people-and-access]

### Role [#role]

Data Hub has two roles, **Member** and **Admin**. Members sign in, browse instruments and runs, claim and comment on runs, send feedback, and read the token list. Admins can also confirm and update instruments, create and revoke tokens, promote or demote other users, delete any comment, review feedback, and manage integrations. Full permission tables are in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles).

### Personal access token [#personal-access-token]

A `dhub_`-prefixed bearer token that authenticates the watcher, and other API clients, with the Data Hub API. Tokens carry permission [scopes](#scope) and are created and revoked by admins. The plaintext is shown once, at creation.

A token acts as itself, under its own name. Comments it posts and runs it deletes show the token’s name with a key icon, not a person. Because a token isn’t a person, it can’t claim runs or send feedback. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

### Scope [#scope]

A permission string carried by a token, such as `runs:read`. A token-authenticated request is refused with `403 FORBIDDEN` when the token’s scopes don’t cover what the route requires. Dashboard sessions hold every scope, so scope checks only apply to token requests. The scope table is in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#token-scopes).

### Feedback report [#feedback-report]

A bug report or feature request about Data Hub itself, sent from the account menu or by an AI assistant. Each report is stored as an issue in your workspace’s Linear, and its status (Open, Resolved, or Declined) follows that issue. See [Send feedback and see what’s new](/docs/send-feedback).
